back: A brief attack triggered by rolling over or looking up favors BPPV. Fluctuating auditory symptoms with spontaneous attacks suggest Ménière disease. Progressive asymmetric hearing loss suggests schwannoma. Related Hazzard 8e, pp. 670, 673–674.

front: What distinguishes carotid sinus syndrome from a hypersensitive response in an older person without spontaneous symptoms?
back: The abnormal response to monitored carotid sinus stimulation reproduces the usual symptoms. A pause or pressure fall alone can occur without a clinical syndrome. Screen for contraindications before testing. Hazzard 8e, pp. 669, 672.

front: Which component of carotid sinus syndrome can a dual-chamber pacemaker treat?
back: A documented cardioinhibitory pause in a selected patient with severe recurrent unpredictable syncope. Pacing maintains rate and AV coordination but cannot directly reverse peripheral vasodilation. Hazzard 8e, p. 675.

front: What do the Dix–Hallpike test and the Epley maneuver each accomplish for posterior-canal BPPV?
back: Dix–Hallpike provokes brief torsional upbeating nystagmus and vertigo. Epley moves canaliths from the posterior canal into the utricle to resolve that abnormal stimulus. Hazzard 8e, pp. 673–674, 676, Figures 45-1 and 45-2.

front: Why can a regular vestibular suppressant prolong symptoms and increase falls in an older adult with chronic dizziness?
back: Suppression can interfere with adaptation, while sedation or anticholinergic effects impair balance. Review the drug and consider supervised vestibular rehabilitation for an appropriate patient. Hazzard 8e, pp. 675–676.

front: אחרי שבר במפרק הירך המטופלת מפסיקה לענות כשבתה בחדר. מה מבררים תחילה?
back: מציעים שיחה ביחידות ובשפתה. בודקים אם היא חוששת לדבר, מה אירע ומה היא צריכה כדי להרגיש בטוחה. השינוי בנוכחות המלווה מכוון לבירור התעמרות נפשית. חוזר 22/03, נספח 1ב, עמ׳ 8, וסעיף 8.1, עמ׳ 6.

front: האם גיל מבוגר ואבחנת דמנציה מספיקים כדי להפעיל את חובת הדיווח על פגיעה בחסר ישע?
back: מבררים אם האדם יכול לדאוג למחייתו, לבריאותו ולשלומו. אם יש במסגרת התפקיד יסוד סביר לחשוב שאחראי עבר בחסר ישע עבירה מהמנויות בחוק, מדווחים בהקדם לעובד סוציאלי שמונה לפי חוק או למשטרה. חוק העונשין, סעיפים 368א ו־368ד(ב),(ח), עמ׳ 57–58 בקובץ.

front: מטופלת רוצה לשוב לביתה לאחר אשפוז עקב החמצת תרופות ויש חשד להזנחה מצד המטפל האחראי. מה קודם לשחרור?
back: מדווחים כאשר מתקיימים תנאי החובה, שומעים את המטופלת ומבררים מי יסייע בפועל. מתאמים פתרון בטוח עם פקידת הסעד והצוות. גם חזרה הביתה עשויה להתאים אם יש מענה לסיכון. חוזר 22/03, סעיפים 8 ו־10, עמ׳ 6.

front: באיזה מצב קובע נוהל משרד הבריאות תקופת אשפוז מזערית של 24 שעות ומהי החלופה?
back: קיים חשד להתעמרות ונדרש אשפוז עקב הפגיעה. סעיף 9 קובע 24 שעות אשפוז לפחות או אמצעי הגנה מיידיים אחרים, בנוסף לדיווח. הצורך הרפואי נבחן בפני עצמו. חוזר 22/03, עמ׳ 6.

front: Practice · Why take the caregiver’s account separately after eliciting the patient’s history?
back: Clarify who provides care, how injuries occurred and what strains or barriers are present. A companion may dominate the interview or retaliate after a confrontation. Interview each privately and seek collateral information. Hazzard 8e, pp. 722–724, Table 48-3.

front: Practice · An older patient needs help with shopping. Does that response alone make EASI positive?
back: The first question establishes dependence. A positive response to any of questions 2 through 6 warrants further assessment. This primary-care instrument was validated in cognitively intact adults and cannot exclude abuse when negative. Hazzard 8e, pp. 722–723, Figure 48-1.

front: US practice · A trusted caregiver has stolen money. What has to be settled before assuming the patient can continue living with him?
back: Assess immediate danger and continuing access to the patient’s money, involve APS, and arrange practical protection. If staying there cannot be made safe, arrange another safe setting. Ask the patient about preferences and assess capacity for each decision. Hazzard 8e, pp. 723–725.

front: A smoker stops after the same two blocks each day. Which treatment improves walking distance, and how should he walk?
back: Support smoking cessation and structured, preferably supervised walking. Walk into tolerable claudication, recover, then repeat. Adjust the pace for balance and other disabilities. The chapter describes about 30 minutes three times a week. Hazzard 8e, p. 1211.

front: When does a short focal arterial stenosis in a claudicant justify angioplasty?
back: Consider it when important activities remain limited despite exercise and medical therapy and the expected functional benefit justifies procedural risk. New rest pain or tissue loss changes the urgency. Related Hazzard 8e, pp. 1210–1212.

front: A frail woman with nephropathy had a TIA and has 50% right internal carotid stenosis. What must be clarified before offering surgery?
back: Confirm a recent matching retinal or hemispheric event. Start medical prevention in every case. Consider endarterectomy selectively at 50%–69% if anticipated benefit exceeds the perioperative and competing risks. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1212–1214.

front: How does an incidental 80% carotid stenosis differ from a symptomatic stenosis when deciding on repair?
back: Intensive medical prevention is foundational. The historical operative option is selected endarterectomy in a low-risk patient with adequate longevity. CREST-2 found a four-year benefit for added stenting and no significant benefit for added endarterectomy in separate trials. Related Hazzard 8e, pp. 1213–1214. CREST-2, Table 2.

front: What trade-off matters when choosing between carotid endarterectomy and transfemoral stenting in an octogenarian?
back: Endarterectomy carries more myocardial infarction and local cranial nerve injury. Transfemoral stenting carries more perioperative stroke, especially with a calcified or tortuous arch. Hazzard 8e, p. 1214.

front: An older patient has bilateral brown pigmentation around the lower shins and ankles. Which test identifies the underlying venous problem?
back: Venous duplex demonstrates venous anatomy and the direction and duration of flow. The chapter considers superficial reflux of at least 0.5 second significant. Chronic venous hypertension causes edema, hemosiderin deposition and sometimes ulceration. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1216–1217.

front: How does statin initiation differ between an 86-year-old smoker without known vascular disease and a 79-year-old with atherosclerotic PAD?
back: PAD is clinical atherosclerotic disease and merits secondary prevention. At 86 without known disease, weigh potential primary-prevention benefit against life expectancy, treatment burden and preferences. The examination cites GRS Cardiovascular Disease. Related Hazzard 8e, p. 1211, and 2026 ACC/AHA Dyslipidemia Guideline, section 4.2.8.3.

front: Which medication can improve persistent walking-limited claudication, and which cardiac condition excludes it?
back: Cilostazol inhibits phosphodiesterase III and can improve walking distance. Avoid it in heart failure of any severity. Continue exercise and vascular prevention. Hazzard 8e, p. 1211, with correction from the 2024 ACC/AHA PAD guideline, section 5.7.

front: What does new foot pain at rest after arterial bypass require you to assess before adjusting analgesia?
back: Check for inadequate perfusion or graft occlusion. Examine temperature, pulses or Doppler signals, sensation and movement. Acute pain with a cold, numb or weak limb requires emergency assessment. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1210–1212.

front: Which anatomical measurement drives elective AAA repair decisions, and what else can shorten the timetable?
back: Maximal aneurysm diameter predicts rupture. Usual repair thresholds are 5.5 cm for men and 5.0 cm for women. Symptoms attributable to the aneurysm or rapid growth can justify earlier intervention. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1215–1216. 2022 ACC/AHA Aortic Disease Guideline, section 6.5.5.3.

front: A man with a 4.8-cm asymptomatic AAA has annual ultrasounds. What changes the timing?
back: New abdominal or back pain potentially attributable to the aneurysm prompts immediate clinical reassessment and appropriate imaging. Ultrasound is preferred for routine follow-up. A stable small aneurysm does not call for stopping aerobic activity or starting doxycycline. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1215–1216, Table 78-2.

front: Which volume remains after a quiet expiration, and why can it rise with age?
back: Functional residual capacity (FRC) is the resting end-expiratory volume. Weaker inward recoil can leave the lung at a higher resting volume. Residual volume is measured after maximal expiration. Hazzard 8e, p1231, explains the recoil and chest-wall mechanics. June 2022 cites Hazzard 7e, pp1236–1237.

front: What happens to FEV1 during healthy aging?
back: It falls. Loss of recoil and earlier closure of the small airways reduce the volume expelled in the first second. The pulmonary teaching is on Hazzard 8e, p1231. The 2023 bibliography prints kidney pages 1280–1281.

front: Why does FEV1/FVC normally decline with age even if total lung capacity is preserved?
back: FEV1 falls proportionately more than FVC. Opposing changes in lung recoil and the chest wall keep TLC relatively stable. Interpret an individual ratio against age-appropriate reference limits. Hazzard 8e, p1231.

front: Which volume rises as small airways close earlier during forced expiration?
back: Residual volume increases because more air is trapped after maximal expiration. Less air is available for expiration, so FVC tends to fall. Hazzard 8e, p1231.

front: Which changes accompany weaker lung recoil and impaired airway clearance?
back: The matrix contains less elastin and more collagen. Airway ciliary movement diminishes. The memory T-cell pool expands while the naïve pool shrinks, and DLCO generally declines. Hazzard 8e, pp1230–1231.

front: An older nonsmoker has insidious dyspnea, fine crackles and interstitial markings on chest radiography. What diagnosis and treatment do these clues suggest?
back: Consider idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, evaluate other causes, and characterize the pattern on high-resolution CT. Nintedanib can slow loss of FVC in established IPF. Hazzard 8e, pp1231–1232. The December 2021 question supplies a chest radiograph.

front: Which measurable benefit can be expected of nintedanib in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
back: A slower rate of loss of FVC. Existing scar persists and breathlessness may continue. Oxygen treats hypoxemia. The treatment paragraph is on Hazzard 8e, p1231. The 2026 examination prints pp1232–1233.

front: Which gastrointestinal effects should you ask about at follow-up after starting an antifibrotic for IPF?
back: Ask about diarrhea, especially with nintedanib, and nausea, especially with pirfenidone. The effect on intake, weight and treatment tolerance guides whether a change is needed. Hazzard 8e, p1231.

front: An 84-year-old asks whether a routine mammogram will help her live longer. What can you say, and what changes if she has a new lump?
back: A breast cancer mortality benefit from routine screening after age 75 is unproven. Discuss competing illness, life expectancy and her wishes. A new lump calls for diagnostic assessment regardless of the screening timetable. Related eighth-edition teaching, pp. 1397–1398, Table 89-1.

front: Late menarche, many births, drinking alcohol or underweight: which increases breast cancer risk?
back: Alcohol. The chapter also identifies early menarche, later first birth, late menopause and postmenopausal obesity as risk factors. Underweight and late menarche reverse the associations presented. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1395–1396.

front: A woman treated for metastatic breast cancer has dysuria and hematuria. Which of cyclophosphamide, letrozole, megestrol and methotrexate points to bladder injury?
back: Cyclophosphamide can cause cystitis, including hemorrhagic cystitis. Letrozole more often causes arthralgia and bone loss, megestrol can cause weight gain, and methotrexate can cause mucositis or renal toxicity. Hazzard 8e, p. 1404, Table 89-4.

front: Which treatment merits left ventricular monitoring: trastuzumab, letrozole, paclitaxel or cyclophosphamide?
back: Trastuzumab can cause cardiomyopathy. Assess left ventricular function before and during therapy. Paclitaxel more typically causes neuropathy, letrozole bone loss and cyclophosphamide cystitis. Hazzard 8e, p. 1404, Table 89-4.

front: After lumpectomy for small, node-negative, hormone-sensitive disease, what does an older woman taking endocrine therapy give up by omitting irradiation?
back: Some local control. At ten years the chapter quotes about ten in-breast recurrences per hundred without radiation and two to three with it. Overall survival was similar in this selected population. Hazzard 8e, p. 1400.

front: Two patients have the same tumor stage. What assessment reveals why one may have more difficulty tolerating or completing treatment?
back: Comprehensive geriatric assessment examines daily function, cognition, comorbidities, medications, nutrition, mood and real-world support. Falls or difficulty organizing treatment can prompt intervention before therapy. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1401–1402.

front: An independently living man with resected estrogen receptor-positive breast cancer needs adjuvant endocrine treatment. Which agent is preferred?
back: Tamoxifen. Its receptor blockade targets hormone-sensitive disease. If contraindicated, an aromatase inhibitor with gonadal suppression is an alternative. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1405–1406.

front: A rural patient lives far from oncology care and lacks reliable transport or language support. Which referral addresses the delay?
back: Patient navigation and social work to arrange transportation, language assistance and access to resources. Make the cancer treatment decision with her once the practical options are clear. Hazzard 8e, p. 1406.

front: Does a symptomatic patient starting treatment for metastatic breast cancer have to wait for hospice to receive palliative care?
back: No. Consider palliative consultation at diagnosis to address symptoms, support the family and discuss goals alongside cancer treatment. Hazzard 8e, p. 1406.

front: For a breast cancer patient with bone metastases, what do denosumab and bisphosphonates protect against?
back: They reduce osteoclast-mediated bone breakdown and the risk of skeletal complications such as pathologic fracture. Focal pain may also benefit from palliative radiation. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1403–1404.

front: A woman with painful vertebral recurrence of hormone receptor-positive breast cancer declines chemotherapy. What options address systemic disease and local pain?
back: Discuss endocrine-based therapy when disease is not rapidly progressive or life-threatening, and assess focal pain for palliative radiation. Her preference about chemotherapy leaves both options open. Hazzard 8e, p. 1403.

front: A patient with pneumonia has hemoglobin of 8.3 g/dL, high ferritin, low transferrin and creatinine of 1.9 mg/dL. What must you establish before prescribing an ESA?
back: Confirm persistent CKD-related anemia and address reversible causes, including inflammation. The exam favors renal anemia with an ESA. A single creatinine cannot establish chronicity. Hazzard 8e, p. 1480, and KDIGO 2026, Figure 5.

front: An independent patient with stable CKD has hemoglobin of 11.1 g/dL and no anemia symptoms. Start an ESA?
back: Monitor the trend and finish assessing correctable causes. An ESA is usually unnecessary at this hemoglobin in stable nondialysis CKD. GRS, Nephrology, Chronic Kidney Disease. Related Hazzard 8e evaluation, p. 1480.

studyReference.label: June 2022 renal case and KDIGO Figure 5

front: During sepsis, serum iron and transferrin fall while ferritin and CRP rise. What is happening to iron?
back: Inflammation raises hepcidin, restricting iron release from stores and availability to the marrow. Treat the infection and reassess. The 2020 exam cites Harrison, pp. 629–630. The corresponding 21e comparison is Table 97-6, p. 753.
sourceLabel: Related causes of anemia · Hazzard 8e, p. 1480

front: Hemoglobin is 8.5 g/dL with normal cell size and iron indices just after hip fracture fixation. Which cause best fits the timing?
back: Perioperative blood loss, with a possible dilutional contribution. Follow serial hemoglobin and assess continued loss if it falls further. GRS, Hematology. Hazzard 8e, p. 1474, explains reduced marrow reserve after bleeding.

studyReference.label: June 2022 hip-fracture case and prospective cohort

sourceLabel: Related marrow response to bleeding · Hazzard 8e, p. 1474

front: Why leave a day between oral iron doses in a stable older adult with iron-deficiency anemia?
back: A dose raises hepcidin for up to 24 hours. The next day, less intestinal iron reaches the blood. Alternate-day dosing avoids that interval and oral therapy is usually sufficient. Hazzard 8e, p. 1480.

front: When should oral iron be replaced by an infusion?
back: Consider intravenous iron when an adequate oral course fails to improve the anemia or adverse effects prevent treatment. Check why the response is poor, including ongoing loss. Hazzard 8e, p. 1480.

front: Which tests distinguish common causes of anemia before you ascribe it to aging or CKD?
back: Start with CBC and differential, reticulocytes, iron indices and ferritin, B12, red-cell folate, creatinine, thyroid and liver function. Select further studies from the findings. Marrow biopsy is warranted when marrow malignancy is suspected. Hazzard 8e, p. 1480.

front: After a negative anemia work-up, how can erythropoietin help explain some cases despite preserved filtration?
back: Some patients produce too little erythropoietin for the degree of anemia despite preserved renal excretory function. Unexplained anemia is a diagnosis of exclusion. Clonal mutations account for only a minority. Hazzard 8e, p. 1480.

front: A patient with chronic anemia now has chest pain and dyspnea on minimal exertion at 7.6 g/dL. What changes?
back: New end-organ ischemia supports prompt transfusion and clinical reassessment. Hazzard gives 8 g/dL in this situation and 7 g/dL as its general threshold. Neither is a universal treatment target. Hazzard 8e, p. 1480.

front: Why might increasing a chronic hemolysis transfusion target from 6 to 7 g/dL make treatment worse?
back: In the chapter’s example the patient functions well at a stable 6 g/dL. Maintaining 7 g/dL increases transfusions without improving quality of life. New symptoms or a falling level would prompt reassessment. Hazzard 8e, p. 1480.

front: A frail patient struggles to attend weekly injection visits. Which outcome should shape anemia treatment?
back: Weigh symptom relief and daily function against adverse effects and the practical burden of treatment. Achieving a normal hemoglobin concentration alone does not justify repeated visits or transfusions. Hazzard 8e, p. 1480.

front: How can an older patient have impaired adaptive immunity and persistent inflammatory signaling at the same time?
back: Inflammaging is systemic, chronic, low-grade inflammation. Senescent T cells proliferate poorly yet may activate inflammatory pathways. In the marrow, IL-1 favors myeloid differentiation and IL-6 promotes platelet production. Hazzard 8e, p. 1479.

front: An 85-year-old entering long-term care cannot document a pneumococcal vaccine. What determines the next step?
back: Check records, then vaccinate according to the schedule for unknown status. Age and chronic heart or lung disease increase the risk of invasive illness. Prior pneumonia does not identify the vaccine needed. Israel introduced PCV20 in place of PCV13 in February 2025. Hazzard 8e, p. 1676, and Israel Ministry of Health.

front: Does a serum albumin of 3.2 g/dL rule out impaired vaccine response? How does low B12 fit?
back: No. Hazzard describes weaker responses in outpatients with albumin 3.0–3.5 g/dL. Low B12 also correlated with weaker pneumococcal polysaccharide antibody responses in a small study. Neither finding predicts an individual vaccine failure. Hazzard 8e, p. 1668, and PMID 8554224.

front: Toxin-positive diarrhea, creatinine 2 mg/dL and blood pressure 82/45 mmHg. Which finding changes the route of CDI therapy?
back: Hypotension indicates fulminant CDI. Give enteral vancomycin with IV metronidazole and resuscitate. If ileus interferes with delivery, consider rectal vancomycin. Assess early for surgical complications. Hazzard 8e, p. 1673, Table 104-1, and SHEA/IDSA Table 1.

front: A stable 87-year-old develops diarrhea and a positive stool toxin on cefuroxime. Is stopping cefuroxime sufficient?
back: Stop unnecessary cefuroxime and treat the active CDI. Oral vancomycin is suitable among the offered drugs. Fidaxomicin is preferred when feasible for initial nonfulminant CDI. Hazzard 8e, p. 1672, Table 104-1, and SHEA/IDSA 2021.

front: Which is the main age-specific difference in CDI: treatment protocol, carriage progressing to symptoms, or recurrence?
back: Recurrence is more frequent in older adults. Severity and prior episodes guide treatment. The chapter estimates about 15% of asymptomatic carriers became symptomatic following antibiotics. Hazzard 8e, p. 1675.

front: A 78-year-old with one resolved CDI episode needs antibiotics for pneumonia. What changed in prevention guidance after June 2026?
back: AGA advises against routine vancomycin during other antibiotics for CDI prevention. Hazzard describes a benefit, and 2021 ACG guidance allowed consideration in selected high-risk patients. Treat new compatible diarrhea if it develops. Hazzard 8e, p. 1675, and AGA 2026, advice 12.

front: After recent admission for CDI, a patient with pneumonia is confused and hypotensive. What do IV and oral vancomycin each contribute?
back: IV vancomycin covers MRSA when risk warrants it. Piperacillin–tazobactam covers susceptible gram-negative pathogens. Oral vancomycin adds no lung activity. Evaluate severe community-onset pneumonia, including atypical coverage and specific resistance risks, separately from CDI prevention. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1673, 1675.

front: In an older patient with prolonged unexplained fever, which inflammatory diseases replace lupus in the differential?
back: Giant cell arteritis with polymyalgia rheumatica and polyarteritis nodosa. In the pooled series temporal arteritis/PMR was the largest individual grouping at 19% of all cases, although infection was the largest overall category. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1675–1676, Table 104-2.

front: Can thrombosis cause fever of unknown origin without recurrent pulmonary embolism?
back: Yes. Deep venous thrombosis can occasionally cause persistent fever with or without recurrent pulmonary emboli. Hematologic cancer, occult infection, vasculitis and drug fever remain important competing explanations. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1675–1676.

front: A BCG-vaccinated older adult has a positive skin test. What can a subsequent IGRA clarify?
back: BCG can produce a false-positive skin test. IGRA is more specific following BCG and needs one blood draw. A positive result still requires assessment for active TB before classifying infection as latent. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1675, 1693–1694.

front: An older adult has new confusion and poor intake without a high temperature. What prevents both missed infection and overtreatment?
back: Recognize that baseline temperature and febrile response may both be lower. Examine for a focus and consider alternative causes. A positive urine culture can reflect asymptomatic bacteriuria. Hazzard 8e, p. 1669.

front: How can a patient need a full first antibiotic dose and a smaller maintenance dose?
back: Rapid therapeutic exposure matters in serious infection. Later drug accumulation depends on clearance, so review renal and hepatic function, interacting drugs and toxicity. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1667, 1670.

front: Which likely source changes empirical coverage in an older adult with sepsis and a chronic urinary catheter?
back: Urinary or gastrointestinal infection makes gram-negative bacilli especially important. Catheter-associated urinary sepsis can also involve enterococci. Select adequate empirical coverage, obtain informative cultures and narrow as results arrive. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1671–1673, Table 104-1.

front: Why obtain cultures before starting antibiotics in stable suspected prosthetic infection?
back: The organism and susceptibility help select therapy and determine whether implant retention is feasible. Distinguish stable patients from those needing immediate sepsis treatment. Consider function, implant stability and surgical risk. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1673–1674.

front: When does antibiotic dosing frequency become a particular adherence concern?
back: Hazzard associates more than two doses per day with poorer adherence. Ask about swallowing, sensory impairment, caregivers and existing medicines before choosing an equally effective simpler schedule. Hazzard 8e, p. 1670.

front: A patient reaches FIM level 6 for walking and transfers, while problem-solving remains at level 2. What should the discharge plan account for?
back: Level 6 means modified independence on those motor tasks. Limited problem-solving and memory can still make supervision necessary, and dressing or bathing may require hands-on help. Hazzard 8e, p. 821, related rehabilitation assessment; December 2021 Q56, FIM table on exam p. 23.

front: In normal aging, which cognitive functions does Table 57-1 list as preserved?
back: Crystallized verbal intelligence, sustained attention and primary attention span, real-world executive functions, remote, procedural and semantic memory, comprehension, vocabulary and syntactic abilities, construction and simple copy. Learning new information, divided attention, word finding and processing speed decline. Hazzard 8e, p. 854.

front: What dominates the early picture of behavioral variant FTLD?
back: A prominent decline in social cognition and behavior and/or executive dysfunction, with at least three of disinhibition, apathy, lost empathy, compulsive behavior and hyperorality. Formal testing and the MMSE may be normal early. Hazzard 8e, p. 873.

front: Which pathology goes with each PPA variant?
back: Although not consistent in every case: agrammatic PPA is often associated with tau, logopenic PPA with Alzheimer pathology, semantic PPA with TDP-43. Hazzard 8e, p. 873.

front: An older adult has progressive asymmetric tremor, rigidity and myoclonus of one hand, ideomotor apraxia and slowed verbal fluency. Which syndrome is this?
back: Corticobasal syndrome, the main phenotype of corticobasal degeneration (tau; asymmetric frontal and parietal atrophy). Mean onset in the early 60s; alien limb is more prevalent; memory is typically well preserved early, unlike AD. Hazzard 8e, p. 874.

front: Why can a patient with logopenic aphasia repeat single words but not sentences?
back: The hypothesized deficit is in short-term working memory; single-word repetition needs little working memory. Speech is usually grammatical and naming is less impaired than in semantic dementia. Hazzard 8e, p. 874.

front: How does the chapter separate PDD from DLB?
back: Printed wording (Hazzard 8e, p. 870): dementia developing after a year of established parkinsonian motor symptoms is PDD. The DLB sentence describes motor symptoms after dementia and adds “or within one year of motor symptom onset” without naming the event in the parenthesis. Standard one-year rule: use DLB when dementia precedes parkinsonism or begins within one year of motor onset; use PDD for later dementia in established PD (DLB Consortium, 2017).

front: Which neurologic signs may appear as prion disease progresses, and what supports the diagnosis?
back: Hyperreflexia, impaired coordination, changes in saccadic eye movements and incontinence. EEG changes, MRI hyperintensities and abnormal CSF 14-3-3 protein. Hazzard 8e, p. 876.

front: Why does palliative care in prion disease often consist largely of hospice care?
back: The course is rapid and diagnosis usually comes late, at moderate-to-advanced stages within months. Care includes hospice, social work for disability and end-of-life decisions, and bereavement support. Hazzard 8e, p. 876.

front: How may syphilitic dementia present, and what does penicillin achieve?
back: Generally 5–25 years after infection, with hallucinations, delusions, mood disturbance, personality change, strokes, ataxia or cognitive decline. There is only limited evidence of cognitive benefit from penicillin. Hazzard 8e, pp. 876–877.

front: Which cognitive pattern is a core feature of DLB?
back: Fluctuating cognition with prominent variations in attention and alertness, alongside recurrent visual hallucinations and spontaneous parkinsonism (Table 63-3). The MMSE typically drops four to five points a year, faster than the three points typical of AD. Hazzard 8e, p. 984.

front: Which drug class should patients with DLB be tried on?
back: Cholinesterase inhibitors; responses often exceed those in AD, including fewer hallucinations. Levodopa can be used if indicated once fluctuation and hallucinations are stabilized; atypical neuroleptics only cautiously if behavior becomes intolerable. Hazzard 8e, p. 984.

front: How common is REM sleep behavior disorder in DLB, PD and MSA?
back: About 85% of DLB, 15% of Parkinson disease and 60% of MSA. It is common to the α-synuclein disorders and is a core DLB feature. Hazzard 8e, p. 983.

front: Which features predict dementia in Parkinson disease?
back: Older age at motor onset, bradykinesia, nontremor-predominant disease, bilateral motor onset and declining response to levodopa; depression and visual hallucinations may add risk. Hazzard 8e, p. 985.

front: How do MSA-P and MSA-C differ in frequency, and what worsens survival?
back: Parkinsonism (MSA-P) predominates in about 80%, cerebellar symptoms (MSA-C) in about 20%. Prominent orthostatic features carry decreased survival; death typically within 6 to 10 years. Hazzard 8e, p. 985.

front: What eye findings mark PSP?
back: Vertical supranuclear gaze palsy (downward more specific), with the oculocephalic reflex preserved early; square wave jerks and saccadic latency and hypometria, greater with command than pursuit. Hazzard 8e, p. 992.

front: What imaging finding does Table 63-5 give for PSP?
back: Dorsal midbrain atrophy with a dilated third ventricle, the hummingbird sign; history buzz words are early falls, impaired vertical gaze and axial rigidity; pathology is tau. Hazzard 8e, p. 993.

front: What characterizes postconcussive syndrome after mild TBI?
back: Headache, dizziness, sleep disturbance, irritability, anxiety, depression, subtle personality change and cognitive complaints in 30% to 80%. The book states that injury severity does not directly correlate with its development; treatment is supportive. Hazzard 8e, p. 995.

front: What does the chapter say about cholinesterase inhibitors in bvFTD?
back: There is no theoretical basis for them and they may worsen agitation; SSRIs for behavioral symptoms and atypical neuroleptics if delusions are problematic. Hazzard 8e, p. 991.

front: What happens to human kidney mass with age?
back: It declines after the fourth decade and through the rest of life, mainly cortex with relative medullary sparing; in most laboratory animals it does not. Hazzard 8e, p. 1271.

front: Which structural changes accompany the aging kidney's decline in function?
back: Thickening of the basement membrane, mesangial expansion and progressive glomerulosclerosis. Hazzard 8e, p. 1268.

front: Why should serum creatinine stay relatively constant with normal aging, and what does a rise mean?
back: Falling muscle mass reduces creatinine production as filtration falls. A creatinine at the upper end of normal already reflects significant decline, so a rise must be taken seriously and drug doses considered. Hazzard 8e, p. 1268.

front: Why are older adults prone to potassium disorders as GFR falls?
back: Fractional potassium excretion does not rise as much as in the young, partly because of lower aldosterone or aldosterone resistance. Hazzard 8e, p. 1270.

front: Which clinical features does the chapter list for hypokalemia?
back: Muscle weakness including proximal weakness and intestinal ileus, cardiac arrhythmias, polyuria and fatigue; many are asymptomatic. Hazzard 8e, p. 1270.

front: What causes spurious hyperkalemia, and what is the next step?
back: Hemolysis from difficult phlebotomy or sample deterioration, severe thrombocytosis, severe leukocytosis or red cell disorders. Obtain a plasma potassium. Hazzard 8e, p. 1271.

front: Why are older patients more susceptible to hyperkalemia?
back: Lower kidney function and muscle mass, altered muscle ion regulation, lower renin and aldosterone, and drugs such as ACE inhibitors, ARBs and potassium-sparing diuretics. Hazzard 8e, p. 1270.

front: How do anti-CCP antibodies compare with IgM rheumatoid factor?
back: As sensitive (70%–78%) and more specific (88%–96%); unlike RF, they do not appear to increase with normal aging, which makes them useful in older patients. Hazzard 8e, p. 1608.

front: What do the 2010 ACR/EULAR RA criteria combine?
back: Joint involvement, serology, acute-phase reactants and symptom duration (Table 101-1); the cohorts had mean ages of 46–58, so their use in late-onset RA is not validated. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1607–1608.

front: What clinical pattern does Table 101-2 give for late-onset RA?
back: More equal sex ratio, acute onset, oligoarticular large proximal joints, systemic features, absent nodules, high ESR and often negative RF. Hazzard 8e, p. 1610.

front: What does RF seropositivity mean in late-onset RA?
back: As in younger patients, more severe disease, more erosions, worse function and increased mortality. Hazzard 8e, p. 1610.

front: What testing precedes anticytokine therapy in RA?
back: Tuberculosis skin testing or an interferon-γ release assay and a chest x-ray, because tuberculosis usually reflects reactivation of latent infection. Hazzard 8e, p. 1617.

front: How does the chapter handle methotrexate around influenza vaccination?
back: Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines are given as for the general population. Stopping methotrexate for 2 weeks after influenza vaccination may improve the response without a significant increase in disease activity. Hazzard 8e, p. 1619.

front: How does late-onset lupus differ from younger-onset lupus?
back: Female to male ratio about 4:1 rather than 9:1, and more cytopenias, serositis and interstitial pneumonitis (Table 101-8). Hazzard 8e, p. 1621.

front: How is dry eye treated in Sjögren syndrome, and which drug is not recommended for sicca?
back: Preservative-free artificial tears, topical low-dose cyclosporine and punctal occlusion. Anti-TNFs are not recommended for sicca symptoms in primary Sjögren syndrome. Hazzard 8e, p. 1623.

front: What posture relieves lumbar spinal stenosis pain?
back: Flexion: sitting or bending forward, as when leaning on a shopping cart. Standing, walking and extension worsen it (Table 102-3). Hazzard 8e, p. 1632.

front: Which level is most often involved in lumbar spinal stenosis?
back: L4-L5, then L3-L4 and L5-S1; acquired stenosis typically presents at 50 or older. Hazzard 8e, p. 1632.

front: How does neurogenic claudication behave on a treadmill versus a bicycle?
back: It is worse on the treadmill and relieved on the bicycle, because flexion widens the canal; vascular claudication is bad on both. Hazzard 8e, p. 1636.

front: Which causes does Table 102-5 link to insidious, progressive, nonpositional back pain?
back: Tumor, infection, nonspinal visceral pain, degenerative disc disease and osteoarthritis. Abrupt onset points to disc herniation, muscle strain, vertebral compression fracture or mechanical low back pain. Hazzard 8e, p. 1634.

front: Which features are imaging red flags in Table 102-7?
back: Age over 70, recent significant trauma (or milder trauma after 50), unexplained weight loss or fever, immunosuppression, cancer history, osteoporosis or prolonged glucocorticoids, progressive or disabling focal neurologic deficits, symptoms lasting more than 6 weeks, and IV drug use. Pain of two weeks alone is not on the list. Hazzard 8e, p. 1636.

front: What is the usual course of a vertebral compression fracture?
back: Only 30% to 40% are symptomatic; pain typically resolves in 4 to 6 weeks, and more than 20% of patients sustain another fracture within 5 years. Hazzard 8e, p. 1631.

front: Which exposures met Hazzard’s historical definition of health care–associated pneumonia?
back: Hospitalization for ≥2 days in the past 90 days, nursing-home or extended-care residence, home infusion, dialysis in the past 30 days, home wound care, or a family member with a multidrug-resistant pathogen (p1682). Current practice: ATS/IDSA retired HCAP as a trigger for broad-spectrum treatment. For community-acquired pneumonia, assess severity and locally validated MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors (2019, question 11).

front: When should Pseudomonas be suspected in an older adult with pneumonia?
back: Severe COPD (FEV1 below 35%), multiple prior antibiotic courses, ICU admission and/or bronchiectasis, or prior colonization; overall it causes only 1% to 2%. Hazzard 8e, p. 1683.

front: What earns a point in CURB-65?
back: Confusion, urea above 44 mg/dL (BUN above 20), respiratory rate of 30 or more, systolic pressure below 90 or diastolic 60 or less, and age 65 or older (Table 105-4). Hazzard 8e, p. 1686.

front: Which severity scores mark the need for admission?
back: PSI class III or higher, or CURB-65 of 2 or more; a short-stay unit suits CURB-65 of 2 or PSI III. Hazzard 8e, p. 1687.

front: Which agents in Tables 105-9 and 105-10 cover Pseudomonas?
back: Piperacillin/tazobactam, imipenem, meropenem, cefepime or ceftazidime, combined with ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, amikacin or tobramycin. Hazzard 8e, p. 1688.

front: What may reduce aspiration pneumonia in at-risk older adults?
back: Oral care, although efficacy in the highest-risk groups such as nursing home residents was not shown in a high-quality randomized study. Hazzard 8e, p. 1690.

front: What causes a false-positive tuberculin skin test, and what can IGRA not tell you?
back: Nontuberculous mycobacteria and BCG vaccination. IGRA cannot separate past from current infection or latent from active TB. Hazzard 8e, p. 1693.

front: Why avoid a quinolone for pneumonia when tuberculosis is suspected?
back: Its tuberculostatic activity may delay the diagnosis of TB. Hazzard 8e, p. 1689.

front: What defines CAUTI in the chapter?
back: A catheter carrier with compatible signs or symptoms (fever, rigors, clear-cut delirium without another cause, suprapubic or flank pain, pelvic pain), or urinary symptoms within 48 hours of removal, together with at least 10^5 cfu/mL in a single catheter specimen. Hazzard 8e, p. 1700.

front: When should asymptomatic bacteriuria be screened for and treated in older adults?
back: Before endoscopic urologic procedures associated with mucosal trauma; otherwise do not screen or treat it. Hazzard 8e, p. 1703.

front: In a PALTC resident without urinary signs or symptoms, which changes should not prompt a UTI evaluation?
back: Behavioral change (other than delirium), functional decline, falls, anorexia or a change in the character of the urine. Hazzard 8e, p. 1705. Odor or color may change with hydration, diet or medicines.

front: What should MRSA in an older adult's urine prompt you to consider?
back: Staphylococcal bacteremia as a potential source; urinary infection can be hematogenous, especially when S aureus grows without an indwelling catheter. Hazzard 8e, pp. 1702, 1707.

front: Which organisms cause UTI in long-term care residents?
back: E coli remains most frequent, followed by Proteus, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Staphylococcus and Pseudomonas; Acinetobacter, Candida and MRSA are less common. More than one organism appears in 10% to 25% of bacteriuric residents. Hazzard 8e, p. 1707.

front: Why are nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin wrong for complicated UTI?
back: They lack adequate renal penetration. Fluoroquinolones are the only oral empiric option, and not where local resistance exceeds 10%; hospitalize severe illness, suspected sepsis or significant frailty. Hazzard 8e, p. 1711.

front: What nitrofurantoin regimen and renal limit does the chapter give?
back: Monohydrate/macrocrystals 100 mg twice daily for 5 days; avoid if creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min. Hazzard 8e, p. 1708. Avoid nitrofurantoin for long-term suppression.

front: In the current GOLD framework, which exacerbation history puts a patient in group E, and when may initial triple therapy be appropriate?
back: One or more moderate or severe exacerbations in the previous 12 months puts a patient in E. Start LABA plus LAMA in most group B or E patients. In group E, consider adding ICS at blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/µL; concomitant asthma calls for ICS. Hazzard 8e, pp1253–1254, uses the earlier ABCD groups. Current practice: GOLD 2027, assessment and initial treatment, PDF pp56 and 79.

front: How is the Rockwood Frailty Index calculated?
back: Divide the number of deficits present by the total number considered. In the version described in Hazzard, the assessment draws on about 70 possible deficits (p620).

front: What distance is walked to test the "slowness" criterion, and what defines an abnormal result?
back: 15-ft walk time; abnormal = slowest 20%, stratified by gender and height (p620).

front: What CD4+ T-cell count thresholds are linked to HIV-related frailty risk?
back: CD4 <350 cells/mm³ (a marker of advanced HIV disease) is independently associated with a frailty-related phenotype; CD4 <100 cells/mm³ is a further risk factor, as are clinical AIDS and previous opportunistic illnesses (p628).

front: What AHI value alone is diagnostic of SDB, and what value defines severe disease?
back: AHI greater than 15/hour, or greater than 5/hour with significant symptoms or related comorbidities. An AHI greater than 30/hour generally indicates severe SDB (p645).

front: Below which EF does Hazzard generally advise against ASV for central sleep apnea in heart failure?
back: Hazzard reports greater mortality with ASV for central sleep apnea in heart failure with EF <45% and generally advises against ASV in this group (p649). Current practice (not the book): SERVE-HF enrolled patients with LVEF ≤45% in symptomatic chronic heart failure with predominantly central sleep apnea. SERVE-HF found higher mortality with its ASV device in this population. The AASM limits consideration of ASV for central apnea in HFrEF to experienced centers with shared decision-making and close follow-up. AASM 2025, recommendation 4

front: What is "augmentation" in RLS pharmacotherapy, and how often does it occur per year on long-acting dopamine agonists?
back: Worsening of RLS — earlier onset, increased intensity, and/or spread to arms/trunk; estimated at 2% to 15% per year, more likely with higher dose and longer duration (p652).

front: What percentage of Stage 2 pressure injuries heal within 60 days, compared to Stage 3/4?
back: 75% of Stage 2 vs only 17% of Stage 3/4 (p689).

front: What proportion of nursing home residents respond to daytime prompted voiding, and how are responders identified?
back: 25%–40% respond well; identified with a 3-day trial of the intervention (p710).

front: What reduction in incontinence episode frequency is typical with bladder-relaxant drug therapy, and how long should a trial run before judging it a failure?
back: Roughly 60%–70% reduction; a 2- to 4-week trial is needed before concluding a drug has failed (p711).

front: What therapy-intensity requirement distinguishes a Medicare-certified inpatient rehab facility from a skilled nursing facility?
back: A US Medicare inpatient rehabilitation facility generally provides 3 hours of therapy on at least 5 days/week, or 15 hours over 7 consecutive days in documented cases. A skilled nursing facility has no equivalent fixed session-intensity requirement (p822, CMS inpatient rehabilitation coverage criteria).

front: What is the MIRE protocol, and how did sensation after treatment compare with placebo?
back: 890-nm near-infrared light pads, 30-minute sessions, three times a week, 12 treatments total; the majority of studies show it is no more effective than placebo in improving sensation (studies are conflicting) (p826).

front: What are the CAM's sensitivity and specificity?
back: Sensitivity 94–100%, specificity 90–95% (p880).

front: In postacute/nursing-home admissions, what fraction of patients meet full CAM criteria for delirium at admission, and what fraction of those admitted with delirium are still delirious a month later?
back: 16% meet full CAM criteria on admission; of those with delirium, over 50% are still delirious 1 month later (p890).

front: In the Framingham study, what percentage of APOE ε4 homozygotes developed AD by age 85, versus noncarriers?
back: 55% of ε4 homozygotes vs. 9% of noncarriers (27% for heterozygotes) (p895).

front: What ARIA (amyloid-related imaging abnormality) rate was seen with high-dose aducanumab, and what fraction of those cases were symptomatic?
back: Hazzard reports ARIA in 34–36% of high-dose participants. Of those with ARIA, approximately 80% were asymptomatic, so about 20% were symptomatic (p911).

front: How common are psychotic symptoms in AD versus in dementia with Lewy bodies or Parkinson disease dementia?
back: 20% to 30% in AD; over 50% in DLB/Parkinson disease dementia (p923).

front: Benzodiazepines are used in what proportion of AD patients despite weak efficacy evidence, and which ones are preferred if used?
back: 8.5% to 20%; short-acting preferred, and glucuronidated agents — oxazepam, temazepam, or lorazepam — are preferable with complex medical comorbidities (p931).

front: What is the "1-year rule" used to distinguish PDD from DLB?
back: In PDD, established motor parkinsonism begins more than one year before dementia. Dementia before, together with, or within one year after parkinsonism fits the DLB timing convention (p939, DLB Consortium 2017).

front: Which ergot dopamine agonists carry a fibrosis risk, and which one has been withdrawn from the US market?
back: Pergolide, bromocriptine, and cabergoline carry fibrosis risk (cardiac valvulopathy, retroperitoneal/pleuropulmonary/pericardial fibrosis); pergolide has been withdrawn from the US market (p944).

front: What is the "1-year rule" used to separate DLB from PDD?
back: Ch 63, p984, prints “predate parkinsonism by 12 months” as the research criterion. This conflicts with the timing described in Ch 57, p870. There, DLB includes dementia preceding or occurring within one year of parkinsonism, and PDD describes dementia after a year of established motor PD. Current practice (not the book): DLB is diagnosed when dementia occurs before or concurrently with parkinsonism; the 1-year rule between onset of dementia and parkinsonism is kept for research DLB-vs-PDD distinction — DLB Consortium (McKeith et al.), 2017.

front: How does the typical MMSE decline rate in DLB compare to AD?
back: DLB declines faster: about 4–5 points/year vs about 3 points/year in AD (p984).

front: What proportion of nfvPPA cases show TDP-43 pathology versus tau pathology at autopsy?
back: About 20% show TDP-43 (usually type A); the majority show tau pathology (CBD most common, then PSP, then Pick) (p988).

front: What is the approximate 3-year survival in ALS, and what is the most common cause of death?
back: About 50% survival at 3 years; aspiration or respiratory failure is the most common cause of death (p991).

front: In PSP, is downward or upward vertical gaze palsy more diagnostically specific, and why?
back: Downward gaze palsy is more specific, because mild vertical gaze limitation is normal with aging (p992).

front: What Rome IV threshold and time frame define chronic constipation?
back: Table 87-1 prints at least two features on >25% of occasions for ≥12 weeks in the last 12 months, including ≤2 bowel movements/week, straining, hard stool, incomplete evacuation, blockage or manual maneuvers (p1354). Current practice (not the book): Rome IV uses fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements weekly and the last-three-month/onset-six-month window. Rome Foundation, C2.

front: Roughly what proportion of North Americans have constipation, and how many meet formal criteria?
back: 12-19% prevalence; about 63 million people in North America meet Rome II criteria (p1354).

front: How prolonged is total gut transit time in bedridden/institutionalized older adults with constipation, versus normal?
back: 6 days to more than 14 days, versus a normal total transit of under 72 hours (p1356).

front: What percentage of Parkinson disease patients meet Rome criteria for constipation, versus age-matched controls?
back: 59% vs 21% in controls (p1360).

front: Why must metoclopramide use in older adults be time-limited, and what limit and interruption does Hazzard describe for continuous treatment?
back: Older adults are particularly susceptible to potentially irreversible tardive dyskinesia. The book advises avoiding continuous metoclopramide for >12 weeks and encourages a two-week drug holiday or a tolerated dose reduction, with tight glucose control when clinically feasible (p1361). Current practice (not the book): The US boxed warning addresses total treatment exposure; a holiday does not reset the 12-week limit. Reglan prescribing information, Boxed Warning.

front: What PVR cutoff and relative risk link constipation to urinary retention in hospitalized older women?
back: PVR >100 mL; constipation increased retention risk 4-fold (p1362).

front: What daily fiber intake does the chapter recommend, and what fluid intake enhanced fiber's effect in trials?
back: Fiber 20-35 g/day (start at 3-4 g/day and titrate); fluid 1.5-2 L/day enhanced fiber's effect in an RCT in adults 18-50, though often impractical for frail older patients (p1370).

front: What are the approximate prevalences of diabetes and of prediabetes among US adults 65 and older?
back: ~27% diabetes, ~50% prediabetes (p1562).

front: What eGFR and albuminuria values define diabetic kidney disease?
back: Usually eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73m² and/or albuminuria >30 mg/g creatinine (p1562).

front: Which guideline provides the "Good/Intermediate/Poor health" framework for individualizing glycemic targets in older adults, and which US standards mirror it?
back: The 2019 Endocrine Society guideline (Table 99-6); a similar framework appears in the ADA 2021 Standards of Care (p1570).

front: Which long-acting sulfonylurea does Hazzard single out for prolonged hypoglycemia?
back: Glyburide, because of its long action (p1579). Current practice: the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria advise avoiding sulfonylureas as first- or second-line unless there are substantial barriers to safer agents. If one is needed, prefer a short-acting agent such as glipizide over glyburide or glimepiride.

front: How long should carotid sinus massage be performed, and when does the maximal heart-rate fall occur?
back: 5 to 10 seconds (massage is done sequentially on each side); the maximal fall in heart rate usually occurs within 5 seconds of the onset of massage (p669).

front: What is the diagnostic yield of a 24-hour ambulatory Holter monitor in an unselected syncope population, and when can longer monitoring help?
back: Only 1% to 2% diagnostic yield in unselected populations; a Holter is useful when symptoms are frequent. An implantable loop recorder can capture an infrequent recurrent episode when arrhythmia remains a concern after the initial assessment (p671–672).

front: What proportion of women and men will suffer a hip fracture by age 90, and what is the lifetime vertebral fracture risk?
back: One-third of women and one-sixth of men will have a hip fracture by age 90; lifetime vertebral fracture risk is about 12% and similar in both sexes (p760).

front: What is a major limitation of the FRAX tool, and which tool addresses it?
back: FRAX does not include falls as a risk factor, which can underestimate risk in frequent fallers; the Garvan tool includes a history of previous falls and reports risk at both 5 and 10 years (p770).

front: How many people in the US have symptomatic OA, and what is its rank among causes of disability?
back: The chapter reports at least 32 million people in the US and about 240 million worldwide. OA ranked third for years lived with disability in the US estimates it cites (p779).

front: By how much is weight loss from obese to normal weight estimated to reduce knee OA incidence, in men vs. women?
back: An estimated 21% in men and 33% in women (p780).

front: What ACR criteria support classifying a patient's joint pain as OA?
back: Age >50 years, <30 minutes of morning stiffness, crepitus, bony enlargement/tenderness on exam, normal inflammatory labs, OA-consistent synovial fluid and negative rheumatoid factor, and radiographic osteophytes (p781).

front: How does bending direction affect OA-related lumbar spinal stenosis symptoms?
back: Symptoms are relieved by bending slightly forward (eg, walking uphill or leaning on a shopping cart) and worsened by bending backward (eg, walking downhill) (p782).

front: Which hand should hold a cane, and what elbow angle is targeted?
back: The hand opposite the affected hip or knee; the elbow should bend approximately 15 to 20 degrees when walking with the cane (p787).

front: What weight-loss target and timeframe are recommended for OA management?
back: More than 5% weight loss achieved within a 20-week period (p786).

front: Which OA drugs do the chapter’s figures recommend against, and where do the two figures disagree?
back: Figure 52-5B (p786) recommends against glucosamine, bisphosphonates, TNF inhibitors and IL-1 receptor antagonists for hand, knee and hip OA. It shows a strong recommendation against chondroitin for knee and hip OA, consistent with p788. For hand OA, Figure 52-4 (p785) shows a conditional recommendation for chondroitin, while Figure 52-5B (p786) shows a conditional recommendation against it. Current practice (not the book): the ACR/AF guideline text conditionally recommends chondroitin sulfate for hand OA and strongly recommends against it for knee or hip OA. ACR/AF OA guideline, 2019.

front: How many intra-articular glucocorticoid injections are recommended within a 6-month period, and roughly how long does the pain relief last?
back: Hazzard advises against more than three injections in six months and describes pain relief lasting up to two months (p789). Current practice (not the book): EULAR cites a customary limit of 3–4 injections in the same joint per year, with limited evidence for a universal safe count.

front: What is the 10-year failure rate of high tibial osteotomy, and what is the surgical procedure of choice for first CMC (thumb base) OA?
back: Approximately 25% failure rate at 10 years for high tibial osteotomy; trapeziectomy is the procedure of choice for first CMC joint OA (p789–790).

front: In normal aging, which type of intelligence is relatively preserved and which declines?
back: Crystallized (verbal) intelligence is relatively preserved; fluid intelligence (flexible reasoning/problem-solving) declines (p853).

front: Which aspect of attention holds up well with normal aging, and which may decline?
back: Sustained attention (vigilance) is preserved; divided attention (attending to more than one thing at once) may decline, though results are mixed (p854).

front: In normal aging, which verbal fluency type declines (semantic or phonemic), and which stays stable?
back: Semantic fluency ("name all the animals you can") declines; phonemic fluency ("words starting with F") generally remains stable (p856).

front: What proportion of patients show postoperative cognitive decline (POCD) after cardiac surgery at hospital discharge, and at 12 months?
back: 30-70% at discharge; still present in 15-25% at 12-month follow-up (p859).

front: What fraction of patients diagnosed with MCI progress to AD, and over what time frame?
back: About 80% progress to AD within 5 to 8 years, converting at roughly 10-15%/year vs 1-2%/year in the general population (p869).

front: What percentage of dementia cases does normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) make up, and what are its shunt-surgery gait/memory outcomes at 6 months vs 5 years?
back: NPH makes up about 6% of dementia cases. At 6 months post-shunt, 83% improve in gait and 46% improve in memory; of surviving shunt cases at 5 years, only 39% remain gait-improved and fewer than 10% still show cognitive improvement (p876).

front: What proportion of people living with diagnosed HIV in the US were aged 50 or older in CDC's 2021 data, and how does the chapter distinguish dementia from milder cognitive deficits?
back: Over half were 50 or older at the end of 2021 in CDC surveillance. The chapter's treated cohorts had an estimated 2–3% progression to HIV-associated dementia, while milder cognitive deficits were more frequent (50–60%, p876).

front: Which features separate corticobasal syndrome from Alzheimer disease early on?
back: Progressive, asymmetric motor signs (tremor, loss of coordination, rigidity, myoclonus), alien limb, and unilateral, most commonly ideomotor, apraxia; memory is typically well preserved early, in contrast to AD (p874).

front: Which PPA variant preserves single-word repetition while sentence repetition fails, and why?
back: Logopenic aphasia. The hypothesized mechanism is a short-term working memory deficit; single-word repetition needs minimal working memory (p874).

front: Distinguish peripheral sensitization from central sensitization in chronic pain pathophysiology.
back: Peripheral sensitization (inflammatory mediators like histamine/bradykinin lowering nociceptor threshold) causes hyperalgesia and spread of pain; central sensitization (maladaptive CNS plasticity) increases synaptic strength of pain pathways and can produce allodynia, where nonpainful stimuli trigger pain (p1056).

front: Which two HLA alleles should prompt genotype screening before starting carbamazepine, and why?
back: HLA-B15:02 is linked to carbamazepine- and oxcarbazepine-associated SJS/TEN. HLA-A31:01 is associated with several carbamazepine hypersensitivity reactions and occurs across multiple ancestries. The genes do not have the same geographic distribution (p1065, CPIC).

front: What are the two fundamental age-related flaws in the GOLD spirometric criteria for COPD?
back: (1) A fixed FEV1/FVC < 0.70 does not distinguish normal age-related airflow limitation from true COPD-related obstruction (often <0.70 in healthy older never-smokers). (2) FEV1 expressed as %Pred assumes spirometric variability is constant across the adult lifespan, which it is not (p1236, p1243).

front: At what GLI Z-score threshold is airflow obstruction (LLN) defined, and what does a Z-score of –2.55 signify?
back: Z-score < –1.64 defines the lower limit of normal (5th percentile). –2.55 corresponds to the 0.5th percentile and is used as a severity threshold (severe FEV1 Z-score < –2.55), and appears as a marker of resistant-organism risk in exacerbations and of risk for uncontrolled symptoms from advanced COPD (p1236, p1243–1244, p1262).

front: What proportion of people with symptoms of chronic bronchitis, and what proportion with physician-diagnosed emphysema/COPD, have normal spirometry?
back: Two-thirds of those with chronic-bronchitis symptoms and half of those with physician-diagnosed emphysema/COPD have normal spirometry (no airflow obstruction) — yet remain at risk for poor outcomes (p1235).

front: What average number of chronic conditions and filled prescriptions per year characterizes a COPD patient?
back: 3.7 chronic conditions and 35 filled prescriptions per year (p1247).

front: What eosinophil threshold favors adding inhaled corticosteroid (ICS) to bronchodilator therapy, and what eosinophil level increases ICS-associated pneumonia risk?
back: Hazzard reports benefit from ICS/LABA with eosinophils ≥300 cells/mL and high symptom burden plus frequent exacerbations (Group D). ICS-associated pneumonia risk rises with <100 cells/mL, older age, frailty, low BMI or high dose. The chapter discusses ICS withdrawal with <300 cells/mL, particularly <100 cells/mL (pp1253–1254). [sic — all three units are printed per mL in the prose; Table 81-7 on p1246 uses cells/µL.] Current practice (not the book): GOLD expresses these eosinophil counts in cells/µL. GOLD Figure 3.10.

front: What peak inspiratory flow (PIF) does a dry powder inhaler (DPI) require, and which device is preferred when PIF is inadequate?
back: DPIs require PIF > 45 L/min. A soft-mist inhaler (SMI) needs only a gentle breath, offering an advantage over DPIs and pMDIs for patients with low PIF or poor "press and breathe" coordination (p1255).

front: What MMSE and EXIT-25 cutoffs predict impaired ability to learn inhaler technique?
back: MMSE < 24, or EXIT-25 ≥ 15 (also inability to draw intersecting pentagons) (p1255).

front: At what prednisone-equivalent dose does delirium risk rise significantly during COPD exacerbation treatment, and what shorter regimen was shown noninferior to a 7–14 day taper?
back: Delirium risk rises above 60 mg/day. A 5-day course of oral prednisone 40 mg/day was noninferior to a conventional 7–14 day taper, with a shorter length of stay (p1236, p1261).

front: What are the three most common bacterial pathogens in acute COPD exacerbations?
back: Haemophilus influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, and Streptococcus pneumoniae (p1259, Table 81-12).

front: What PaO2/SpO2 thresholds indicate daily long-term oxygen therapy (LTOT), and how many hours per day are needed for a survival benefit?
back: Resting PaO2 ≤ 55 mm Hg or SpO2 ≤ 88% (or PaO2 ≤ 59/SpO2 ≤ 89% with cor pulmonale, pulmonary hypertension, or erythrocytosis). LTOT worn more than 16 hours per day improves survival (p1256).

front: What FEV1/DLCO and homogeneity findings make a patient a poor candidate for lung volume reduction surgery (LVRS)?
back: Hazzard says surgical LVRS should be avoided when FEV1 or DLCO is <20% predicted and emphysema is homogeneous because postoperative mortality is higher (p1258). Current practice (not the book): In NETT, FEV₁ at most 20% predicted plus either homogeneous emphysema or DLCO at most 20% predicted identified patients at high surgical risk. The 30-day mortality was 16% after surgery versus 0% with medical treatment. Original NETT analysis.

front: What BODE Index score threshold, and what FEV1/DLCO percentage, triggers lung transplant referral consideration?
back: BODE Index score > 5, and FEV1 and DLCO both < 25% predicted, among other criteria (PaCO2 > 50 mmHg, PaO2 < 60 mmHg, pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale, ≥1 hospitalization with acute hypercapnia or ≥3 severe exacerbations in the prior year) (p1258–1259).

front: How does average life expectancy from diagnosis compare between COPD and heart disease?
back: 14 years for COPD vs 21 years for heart disease (p1262).

front: What is the sick-day glucocorticoid rule for a patient with known adrenal insufficiency?
back: Triple the usual daily hydrocortisone dose (about 60 mg total) for 3 days with a fever ≥101.5°F; give 100 mg IM hydrocortisone if oral intake is not possible (p1526, p1531–1532).

front: What serum prolactin range defines "mild" hyperprolactinemia that generally does not need treatment, and what should still be checked?
back: 20–50 ng/mL; check a serum TSH to exclude primary hypothyroidism as the cause (p1525, p1528).

front: Which drug can interfere with the aldosterone-to-renin ratio, and what washout can be used when clinically safe?
back: Spironolactone for 4 weeks if safe and feasible. Monitor potassium and blood pressure and arrange alternative therapy when needed (pages 1532–1533).

front: In the Testosterone Trials, what was the baseline testosterone cutoff and the treatment target range?
back: Baseline total testosterone <275 ng/dL; testosterone dosed to a target of 500–800 ng/dL (p1534–1535).

front: What laboratory and skeletal thresholds does Hazzard give for parathyroidectomy, and how do the current renal thresholds differ?
back: The book gives serum calcium >1 mg/dL above the upper limit of normal, T-score <−2.5, creatinine clearance <60 mL/min or 24-hour urine calcium >400 mg (pp1526, 1538–1539). For asymptomatic primary hyperparathyroidism, the Fifth International Workshop uses 24-hour urine calcium >250 mg in women or >300 mg in men and a T-score ≤−2.5 (2022, recommendation 5.1).

front: What is the safe upper limit of daily vitamin D3 intake per the Institute of Medicine, and above what level does early biochemical toxicity appear?
back: Safe upper limit 4000 IU/day; early biochemical indications of toxicity have been reported when 25-hydroxyvitamin D exceeded 90 ng/mL (the first indication of over-treatment is hypercalciuria) (p1540).

front: What is the treatment of choice for Paget disease, and what renal function cutoff contraindicates it?
back: Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV (often a single dose); contraindicated if creatinine clearance <35 mL/min (p1542).

front: By roughly what factor does T4 secretion exceed T3 secretion from the thyroid, and what fraction of each circulates free?
back: T4 secretion is about 11× that of T3. Only 0.04% of T4 and 0.4% of T3 circulate free (biologically active); the rest is protein-bound (p1545).

front: How does the reference range for "normal" TSH differ between a 25-year-old and an 85-year-old?
back: Upper limit of normal is about 3.6 mIU/L at age 20-29 versus 7.5 mIU/L at age 80+, when the 95% confidence interval is applied to a population free of thyroid disease (p1554).

front: What are the two distinct mechanisms by which amiodarone can cause thyrotoxicosis, and how are they treated differently?
back: Increased thyroid hormone production in an underlying nodular or Graves gland is treated with methimazole; destructive thyroiditis from a direct toxic effect is treated acutely with corticosteroids. They can be hard to tell apart, so patients may initially get both. In most cases amiodarone should not be stopped (p1547-1548).

front: What is the mortality rate associated with the full constellation of thyroid-test abnormalities in nonthyroidal illness syndrome, and should it be treated with thyroid hormone?
back: Mortality is about 80% with the full pattern; thyroid hormone replacement (T4 or T3) gives no benefit (p1548).

front: In older patients with overt hyperthyroidism, which three signs reach at least 50% prevalence, and how does this differ from younger patients?
back: Tachycardia (71%), fatigue (56%), and weight loss (50%) (Table 98-3, p1549). Classic hyperadrenergic signs (tremor, sweating, nervousness, heat intolerance) are far less common than in young patients — "apathetic hyperthyroidism" (p1549).

front: Why is methimazole generally preferred over propylthiouracil (PTU) for Graves disease, and what are their shared adverse-effect rates?
back: Methimazole has a longer half-life and fewer adverse effects; PTU carries a risk of fulminant hepatic failure. Both cause skin reactions in 4-6% and agranulocytosis in 0.1-0.5% of patients (p1550).

front: In older patients with overt hypothyroidism, which two signs exceed 50% prevalence?
back: Fatigue (68%) and weakness (53%) — the only two of 24 signs studied that exceeded 50% (p1551).

front: What levothyroxine dosing approach is recommended for a 70-year-old with cardiac disease starting treatment for hypothyroidism, and when should TSH be rechecked?
back: Hazzard names 25- and 50-μg tablets as reasonable initial levothyroxine doses in older adults. TSH testing usually occurs at 6 weeks after initiation (6 half-lives), though older patients may need 7-8 weeks to reach steady state; target TSH toward the upper-normal range, up to 4-6 mU/L if over age 80 (p1552). Current practice (not the book): For stable primary hypothyroidism with known coronary artery disease, start oral levothyroxine at 12.5–25 μg daily and titrate gradually according to cardiac symptoms and TSH (ATA section 4b). ATA, section 4b.

front: What proportion of older adults on thyroid hormone replacement have a low TSH from overreplacement, and what are the associated risks?
back: Up to 40%. Risks mirror endogenous hyperthyroidism, most notably atrial fibrillation and bone loss (p1552).

front: At what TSH threshold is treatment of subclinical hypothyroidism recommended in a patient aged 65 or older, and at what threshold should it be considered?
back: Treat if TSH is persistently ≥10.0 mU/L; consider treatment if TSH is 7.0-9.9 mU/L (p1553-1554). (Figure 98-4, p1554, uses mU/L; the prose on p1553 misprints mU/mL.)

front: What thyroid nodule characteristics indicate FNA is required versus not required (Table 98-8)?
back: FNA indicated: nodules ≥1 cm that are solid and hypoechoic, ≥1.5 cm isoechoic/hyperechoic solid, or abnormal cervical lymph nodes. FNA or observation: mixed cystic-solid or spongiform nodules ≥2 cm. FNA not required: purely cystic nodules or nodules <1 cm; low TSH prompts radionuclide scanning, and functioning hot nodules do not require cytologic evaluation (p1555).

front: What is the median survival for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma, and why does radioactive iodine not work for medullary thyroid carcinoma?
back: Median survival for anaplastic thyroid carcinoma is about 5 months. Radioactive iodine has no effect on medullary thyroid carcinoma because the C-cells do not contain the sodium-iodide symporter (NIS) (p1556).

front: How does the male:female ratio of RA differ between typical (younger-onset) RA and LORA?
back: Typical RA affects women 2–3× more than men, but the female predominance narrows in late-onset disease (p1608) — LORA occurs with roughly equal frequency in men and women (p1610).

front: What joint pattern and demographic features characterize LORA (Table 101-2)?
back: Acute-onset oligoarticular disease (2–6 joints), involvement of large/proximal joints, systemic symptoms (e.g., weight loss), absence of rheumatoid nodules, common sicca symptoms, and a roughly 1:1 male:female ratio (p1610).

front: What is RS3PE syndrome and how does it typically respond to treatment?
back: Remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting edema — affects older men (2–3:1), RF/ANA negative, high ESR, and generally responds well to low-dose prednisone (p1610–1611).

front: At what glucocorticoid doses, and with what relative infection risks, did Medicare beneficiaries over 75 with RA show increased serious-infection rates?
back: For Medicare beneficiaries with RA older than 75, p1618 reports 20%, 32% and 47% increased risk of serious infection at ≤5, >5–10 and >10 mg/day, respectively, and 13% risk without glucocorticoids (printed wording). Current practice (not the book): in the source (Medicare RA patients ≥75 y on stable DMARDs) 12.8/20.0/32.0/46.8 are crude hospitalized-infection rates per 100 person-years, not % increased risk; adjusted HRs vs no glucocorticoid 1.31, 1.74, 2.23 — George et al., Ann Intern Med 2020, Table 3.

front: How is late-onset lupus (LOL) defined, and what fraction of all SLE cases does it represent?
back: Onset of symptoms after age 55; it represents approximately 10% of all lupus cases (p1619).

front: When was belimumab first approved, and when was its indication expanded to lupus nephritis?
back: Hazzard dates initial FDA approval to 2011 and the expanded active lupus nephritis indication to 2021 (pp1621–1622). Current practice (not the book): the US supplemental approval was issued in December 2020 — FDA approval letter, 2020.

front: What are the diagnostic thresholds for a positive Schirmer test and a positive minor salivary gland biopsy in Sjögren syndrome?
back: Schirmer test: less than 5 mm of filter paper wet after 5 minutes. Minor salivary gland biopsy: more than one focus (an aggregate of ≥50 lymphocytes) per 4 mm² of tissue (p1622). Current practice (not the book): 2016 ACR/EULAR primary Sjögren criteria use Schirmer ≤5 mm/5 min and focus score ≥1 focus/4 mm² — Shiboski et al., Arthritis Rheumatol 2017.

front: What dose thresholds define higher risk for hydralazine-induced lupus (HIL)?
back: Risk is dose-dependent and highest in patients taking more than 200 mg/day or with a cumulative dose over 100 g (p1625).

front: What is the most common rheumatic syndrome associated with malignancy, and which cancer most often causes it?
back: Hypertrophic osteoarthropathy — almost always caused by metastatic lung cancer in the Western world (p1625).

front: What historical clue helps differentiate an osteoporotic sacral (insufficiency) fracture, and how often is there a preceding fall?
back: Persistent low back/groin/buttock pain with marked tenderness on sacral pressure; about 50% of patients had a preceding fall (p1631).

front: What is the most common spinal level for lumbar spinal stenosis, and which nerve root is most often affected?
back: L4-L5 most common (followed by L3-L4 and L5-S1); lateral recess stenosis there most often causes an L5 radiculopathy (p1632).

front: After what age does lumbar disc herniation become less common, and why?
back: Beyond age 55, because the nucleus pulposus loses water content with aging (p1633).

front: What defines diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis (DISH) radiographically?
back: Flowing calcification/ossification along the anterolateral aspect of at least 4 contiguous vertebral bodies, with relative preservation of disc height and no apophyseal joint ankylosis (p1633).

front: List the passive hip range-of-motion benchmarks used to help distinguish hip from back pathology.
back: 40 degrees of abduction before the pelvis tilts, more than 100 degrees of flexion, 50–60 degrees of external rotation, and 20 degrees of internal rotation (p1634).

front: What is the reported complication rate range for lumbar decompressive surgery, and name 3 complication types?
back: 1.8% to 18%; complications include wound infection, durotomy, nerve root injury, vascular complications, epidural hematoma, implant failure, adjacent-segment degeneration, and nonunion (p1639).

front: In what fraction of older adults with serious infection is fever absent, and when can lower temperatures indicate fever in a nursing-home resident?
back: Up to one-third may have a serious infection without reaching the conventional 38°C threshold (p1669). Current practice (not the book): For nursing-home residents, a single oral temperature above 37.8°C, repeated oral temperatures above 37.2°C, or a rise above usual temperature of more than 1.1°C can identify fever earlier. IDSA long-term-care fever guideline.

front: What two culture practices should almost always be avoided in older adults, and why?
back: Hazzard says that, almost universally, skin surface swabs and urine cultures in patients with a long-term indwelling catheter should be avoided. Colonization makes these results misleading for antibiotic selection (Key Clinical Point 3, p1667; p1671). Current practice (not the book): For suspected symptomatic CAUTI, IDSA advises culture before antibiotics when feasible. If the catheter is replaced, culture urine from the freshly placed catheter. IDSA, recommendations 45–46.

front: Compare fever and leukocytosis rates in infective endocarditis for older vs younger adults, and state how much TEE improves diagnostic yield over TTE in seniors.
back: Older adults: fever 55%, leukocytosis 25% (vs 80%/60% in younger adults) — a blunter presentation. TEE improves diagnostic yield by 45% over TTE in older adults (p1671).

front: What organisms predominate in early (<60 day) vs late (>60 day) prosthetic device infections?
back: Early: skin flora — coagulase-negative staphylococci, S aureus, diphtheroids. Late: more likely asymptomatic bacteremia seeding the implant, so a wider array of organisms including GI/GU sources, though skin organisms (staphylococci) still predominate (p1671, p1674).

front: What defines a "high risk" prosthetic joint for the historical discussion of dental prophylaxis, and how does current US guidance differ?
back: PJ placed within 2 years, immunosuppressed patients (diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, malnourishment), or a history of prior joint infection (p1674–1675). Current practice note

front: What are the asymptomatic C difficile carriage rates in the community, outpatient-exposed community, and hospital/long-term care settings?
back: 2% community, 10% community with outpatient healthcare exposure, 20–50% hospital or long-term care (p1675).

front: What proportion of asymptomatic C difficile carriers develop symptomatic CDI after receiving antibiotics, and what is the success rate of FMT for refractory relapse?
back: About 15% develop symptomatic CDI; FMT success rate is 80–90% (p1675).

front: What is the classic definition of fever of unknown origin (FUO)?
back: Temperature >101°F (38.3°C) for at least 3 weeks, undiagnosed after 1 week of medical evaluation (p1675).

front: In older adults, what fraction of FUO is ultimately autoimmune, and which two conditions replace SLE as the leading autoimmune causes?
back: Nearly one in four; giant cell arteritis (GCA) and polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) replace SLE, which is essentially absent as a cause of FUO in older cohorts (p1675).

front: What percentage of FUO cases in older patients falls into each of the five major categories in Table 104-2?
back: Infections 35%, inflammatory disorders 28%, malignancy 19%, other causes (pulmonary emboli or drug fever) 5%, and no diagnosis 13% (Table 104-2, p1675).

front: Which three vaccine examples illustrate protective immune responses in older adults in this chapter?
back: High-dose influenza vaccine, adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine, and mRNA-based SARS-CoV-2 vaccines (p1668, p1676).

front: What four items make up the Shorr MDRO risk score, and what does a score of zero mean?
back: Recent hospitalization (4 pts), admission from long-term care (3 pts), hemodialysis (2 pts), critical illness (1 pt); a score of 0 carries an 84% negative predictive value for MDRO (p1682).

front: What rates of ESBL-producing Klebsiella were found among pneumonia isolates in the US vs Europe?
In what fraction of cases can the initial chest x-ray be falsely negative, and what should be done if suspicion for pneumonia remains?
back: Up to 30% (more often with dehydration or neutropenia); repeat the film at 24-48 hours (p1684).

front: What are the sensitivity/specificity of the pneumococcal urinary antigen test, and what limits its use in relapse or treatment-response assessment?
back: Sensitivity >60%, specificity >90%; it stays positive for about 3 months after resolution of the pneumonia (p1685).

front: What vital-sign criteria define readiness for hospital discharge, and by what day do most patients stabilize?
back: HR <100 bpm, RR <24/min, axillary temperature <37.2°C (<98.96°F), systolic BP >90 mm Hg, SpO2 >90%, good awareness and oral tolerance; most stabilize by hospital day 3-4 (up to 7 days if frail) (p1687).

front: How is antibiotic treatment failure defined, and what mortality risk does it carry?
back: No clinical stability by 3-4 days, or deterioration/respiratory failure/septic shock in the first 72 hours; associated with a fivefold increase in mortality. But in older patients with severe pneumonia or serious comorbidity (eg, severe COPD, untreated heart failure), stability may take longer without implying therapeutic failure (p1690).

front: What duration of antibiotic therapy is sufficient for most older adults with pneumonia, and when should it be extended?
