back: 5-7 days; extend for infection by Legionella, resistant gram-negative bacilli, or MRSA, or for persistent fever beyond 72 hours, persistence of more than one criterion of clinical instability, inadequate initial coverage, or complications (p1690).

front: Roughly what fraction of the world's population is estimated to be infected with M tuberculosis, and what is the bimodal age pattern of TB incidence?
back: About 25% (>1.7 billion people); incidence peaks at 15-35 years and again after 65 years (p1691).

front: What is the two-step tuberculin test protocol in older adults, and why is it used?
back: Older adults have increased cutaneous anergy; if the first TST is negative (induration <10 mm), a second test is done at 2 weeks. A positive result is induration ≥10 mm and an increase of ≥6 mm over the first test (p1693).

front: What isoniazid hepatotoxicity rate is seen in patients over 65, compared with those under 65?
back: Up to 4%-5% in patients >65 years, versus <1% in those <65 years (p1694).

front: At what bilirubin or transaminase thresholds should hepatotoxic TB drugs be stopped?
back: Bilirubin ≥3 mg/dL, or transaminases >5x the upper limit of normal (>3x ULN if the patient has symptoms of hepatitis) (p1696).

front: Roughly how many older US adults die from influenza each year, and which influenza types are clinically relevant?
back: About 36,000/year; only types A and B are clinically relevant (type C is not) (p1733).

front: What is the biological difference between antigenic "drift" and antigenic "shift," and which one carries pandemic risk?
back: Drift = annual mutations causing small changes in hemagglutinin (why the vaccine needs yearly reformulation). Shift = recombination of whole RNA segments (the virus has 8) with an animal-origin strain, creating a novel genotype with little/no preexisting immunity — this is the pandemic-risk mechanism (p1733).

front: Which hemagglutinin and neuraminidase subtypes currently have stable human lineages, and which pandemic years resulted from antigenic shift?
back: H1, H2, H3 and N1, N2; shift pandemics occurred in 1957–1958, 1968–1969, and 2009 (p1734).

front: Compare influenza hospitalization rates in older adults vs. those aged 5–49.
back: 136–508 per 100,000 in older adults vs. 10–25 per 100,000 in the 5–49 age group (p1734).

front: Why is a negative rapid antigen test insufficient to rule out influenza in an older adult, and what test should be used instead?
back: Rapid antigen/ELISA tests are insensitive in older adults (sensitivity as low as 20%), so a negative result does not exclude infection. RT-PCR is more than 90–95% sensitive and is the preferred test (p1733, p1735).

front: What vaccine-effectiveness range was found for seasons of vaccine/strain match vs. mismatch in the 2014 systematic review?
back: 38–70% during match seasons, 15–59% during mismatch seasons — described as an important but modest effect (p1735).

front: How does the high-dose influenza vaccine (HD-IIV4) differ from standard-dose (SD-IIV4), and what were the results of the zanamivir-vs-rimantadine nursing-home prophylaxis trial?
back: HD-IIV4 contains 4× the antigen dose per component and generates higher antibody levels/effectiveness in older adults. In the RCT, zanamivir chemoprophylaxis cut influenza risk to 3% vs. 8% with rimantadine (p = 0.038) (p1735).

front: Within what time window do neuraminidase inhibitors (zanamivir/oseltamivir) reduce clinical severity when used as treatment, and what is their approximate prophylactic effectiveness?
back: Treatment reduces clinical severity if given within 48 hours of symptom onset (the book's stated window, not an absolute cutoff — ch105 p1689 adds oseltamivir in severe CAP even after 48 h); about 70–90% effective for prophylaxis (p1736).

front: How do RSV viral shedding titers and duration differ between infants and adults?
back: Infants shed higher titers (10⁵⁻⁶ pfu/mL) for longer (10–14 days); adults shed lower titers (10²⁻³ pfu/mL) for a shorter period (3–6 days) (p1737).

front: In the Rochester community cohort, what proportion of high-risk older adults (CHF or chronic pulmonary disease) developed RSV, and what fraction were hospitalized?
back: 10% (56 high-risk participants, a group separate from the 608 healthy participants, of whom 46 [8%] developed RSV); 16% of high-risk participants with RSV required hospitalization (p1737).

front: What is the only licensed antiviral for RSV, and what limits its practical use in older adults?
back: Ribavirin — it is aerosolized (hard to deliver via face mask to older adults), teratogenic (a hazard to caregivers/family), and supported by only sparse adult efficacy data; care is otherwise supportive only (p1737).

front: Which receptor does SARS-CoV-2 use to enter cells, and why does its upper-respiratory-tract tropism matter for transmission?
back: The ACE2 receptor. Unlike SARS-CoV/MERS (which replicate mainly in the lower respiratory tract), SARS-CoV-2 achieves high viral loads in the upper respiratory tract, and shedding peaks at the very start of infection — enabling presymptomatic spread; the early modeling estimate of 79% concerned previously undocumented infections, including infections with mild symptoms (p1738).

front: What proportion of COVID-19 patients in one study (mean age 81) presented with atypical symptoms, and what did those look like?
back: 40% — presenting with falls, generalized weakness, and delirium rather than the classic fever/cough/fatigue/dyspnea picture (p1738).

front: What did the Clinical Frailty Scale predict better than age or comorbidity alone, and what fraction of COVID-19 deaths occurred in the postacute/long-term care sector despite its small share of cases?
back: The CFS was a better predictor of 7-day mortality in hospitalized SARS-CoV-2 patients than age or comorbidity alone. The postacute/LTC sector accounted for over a quarter (>25%) of deaths despite only about 2% of total confirmed cases (as of November 2020) (p1739).

front: What three screening-tool thresholds trigger the suicide/safety risk factor checklist?
back: PHQ Question 9 ≥1, MADRS Question 10 ≥3, or QIDS-SR Question 12 ≥1 (p1013).

front: What is the typical initial ECT course (frequency and duration), and what happens to short-term memory loss?
back: The average initial course in Hazzard is 3–6 treatments per week for 2–4 weeks. Short-term memory loss almost always resolves within a few weeks after the course ends (p1014). Current practice note

front: How should antidepressant tapering be individualized, and how does fluoxetine's long half-life affect dose reduction?
back: Hazzard gives 2–4 weeks for most SSRIs, SNRIs and mirtazapine and several months for tricyclics. It states that fluoxetine does not require tapering. For symptoms despite a long taper, the chapter suggests considering one dose of fluoxetine 20 mg (p1016). Current practice note

front: In patients older than 65, what fraction of aortic stenosis is caused by calcific degeneration of a trileaflet valve, and at what age does a bicuspid valve's stenosis typically present?
back: 90% of AS in patients over 65 is calcific degeneration of a tricuspid valve; bicuspid-valve stenosis usually presents earlier, in the fourth to sixth decade (p1149).

front: Name the classic triad of symptoms once aortic stenosis becomes symptomatic, and rank them by average survival without valve replacement.
back: Angina (50% 5-yr survival), syncope (50% 3-yr mortality), and heart failure (~50% mortality at 2 years — the worst prognosis of the three) (p1151).

front: On exercise testing, what result predicts a poor 2-year symptom-free survival in "asymptomatic" severe aortic stenosis, and what are the two survival rates?
back: Development of symptoms, failure to generate a 20 mmHg increase in blood pressure, or ST-segment abnormalities predicts a 19% 2-year symptom-free survival, versus 85% if none of these occur (p1151).

front: What STS risk cutoff defines "prohibitive" surgical risk for TAVR consideration, and what is the durability caveat for TAVR valves?
back: Hazzard defines prohibitive SAVR risk as STS predicted morbidity and mortality >50% due to comorbidity or serious irreversible conditions. It describes TAVR valve durability beyond five years as unknown (p1153). Current practice (not the book): the NOTION randomized trial subsequently reported 10-year outcomes in lower-risk patients — NOTION follow-up, 2024.

front: What annual rate of LV dysfunction, symptoms or death was reported in asymptomatic aortic insufficiency with an end-systolic dimension greater than 50 mm, versus 40–50 mm?
back: 19%/year if LVESD > 50 mm, versus 6%/year if LVESD is 40–50 mm (p1153).

front: In asymptomatic severe aortic regurgitation with preserved LV function, how do LV end-systolic and progressive LV enlargement affect referral for surgery?
back: Table 75-6 lists LVESD >50 mm as a reason to consider surgery and progressive LV dilatation >65 mm as a possible indication when surgical risk is low. The table leaves the latter dimension unspecified; the accompanying prose calls it LVESD (p1155). Current practice note

front: What mitral valve area range typically corresponds to symptom onset in mitral stenosis, and what is the normal MVA?
back: Symptoms usually develop once the valve area falls to 2.5–1.5 cm²; normal MVA is 4.0–5.0 cm² (p1156).

front: In mitral stenosis, how does 10-year survival compare between patients who remain in sinus rhythm and those who develop atrial fibrillation?
back: 46% 10-year survival in sinus rhythm versus 25% with atrial fibrillation (p1156).

front: What echocardiographic scoring system selects patients for percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty, and what features give the most favorable (lowest) score?
back: The Wilkins Score; the lowest (most favorable) scores go to valves with the greatest leaflet mobility, least subvalvular thickening, most normal leaflet thickness, and least calcification (p1157).

front: What is the most common cause of mitral regurgitation, and roughly what fraction of the population does it affect?
back: Mitral valve prolapse, present in 1% to 2.5% of the population (p1158).

front: Compare operative mortality for mitral valve repair versus replacement, both in the overall population and in a cohort of patients older than 70.
back: Overall: 2% (repair) vs 6% (replacement). In a 292-patient cohort older than 70: 0.7% (repair) vs 14% (replacement) in-hospital mortality (p1160).

front: What INR range and duration of anticoagulation apply to a bioprosthetic aortic valve without additional risk factors?
back: Table 75-15 gives INR 2–3 for the first 3 months plus aspirin 75–100 mg daily after bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement without additional risk factors. For a mechanical aortic valve it gives INR 2–3, increasing to 2.5–3.5 with thromboembolic risk factors, plus aspirin 75–325 mg daily (p1161). Current practice (not the book): ACC/AHA considers VKA to a target INR of 2.5 for 3–6 months reasonable after selected surgical bioprosthetic aortic or mitral replacement — ACC/AHA 2020.

front: Before elective surgery, how long can warfarin be held preoperatively in a patient with a mechanical aortic valve and no risk factors, and when is it restarted — with or without heparin bridging?
back: Hazzard gives a 48–72-hour preoperative hold for a mechanical aortic valve without thromboembolic risk factors. Restart warfarin within 24 hours after surgery. In this setting the book specifies no bridging heparin (p1162). Current practice note

front: Which oral regimens does Table 75-14 give for dental endocarditis prophylaxis in an eligible patient with penicillin allergy?
back: The printed table lists clindamycin 600 mg PO or cephalexin 2 g PO, given once 1 hour before the procedure (Table 75-14, p1161). Current practice (not the book): AHA dental guidance removes clindamycin. For eligible adults with penicillin allergy, give cephalexin 2 g, azithromycin or clarithromycin 500 mg, or doxycycline 100 mg PO 30–60 minutes before the procedure. Avoid cephalosporins after anaphylaxis, angioedema or urticaria with penicillin or ampicillin. AHA prevention card, dental regimens based on the 2021 scientific statement.

front: What US heart failure prevalence did Hazzard report, and how many affected adults did the projection anticipate by 2030?
back: Hazzard reported about 6.5 million US patients and projected over 8 million by 2030 (p1166). Both figures refer to the chapter's reporting period and forecast.

front: Of 2014 primary-HF hospital admissions, what fraction occurred in patients 75 years or older, and what fraction in the (much smaller) population aged 85 and up?
back: 53% were in patients ≥75y; 25% occurred in the 2% of the population aged ≥85y (p1166).

front: Name the four principal age-related changes in the cardiovascular system that predispose to heart failure.
back: (1) Reduced β-adrenergic responsiveness (receptor desensitization), (2) increased arterial stiffness/afterload, (3) altered left ventricular diastolic filling with increased reliance on atrial contraction, (4) altered mitochondrial energy metabolism under stress (p1166–1170).

front: What BNP cutoffs make heart failure highly likely versus much less likely in a nonobese older adult, and why does BNP become a less reliable rule-in test with age?
back: A BNP above 500 pg/mL strongly supports active heart failure in the appropriate clinical context. A BNP below 100 pg/mL makes heart failure much less likely in a nonobese older adult. Natriuretic peptide levels rise modestly with normal aging (especially in women) and with declining renal function, so specificity for HF declines with age (p1174).

front: The chapter gives a general EF range for HFREF, then a narrower working cutoff. What are the two numbers?
back: General range: "less than 40% to 50%." Working cutoff adopted for the rest of the chapter's discussion: EF <45% for HFREF (HFPEF is ≥45%) (p1175).

front: Which three β-blockers are proven, evidence-based agents for HFREF, and what are their target maintenance doses?
back: Carvedilol 25–50 mg BID, metoprolol succinate 100–200 mg daily, bisoprolol 10 mg daily (p1179).

front: Which renal and potassium findings does Hazzard list as contraindications to an MRA in HFrEF, and what spironolactone dose range does it give?
back: Hazzard lists creatinine ≥2.5 mg/dL or preexisting hyperkalemia as contraindications. It calls for close monitoring of renal function and serum potassium in older patients. The spironolactone dose is 12.5–50 mg once daily (p1181). Current practice note

front: What target serum digoxin concentration is associated with improved survival in HFREF, and does digoxin reduce mortality?
back: 0.5–0.9 ng/mL (DIG analyses: low-dose levels in this range may be associated with improved survival); no — digoxin reduced HF hospitalizations in the DIG trial but did not reduce mortality (34.8% vs 35.1%, not different from placebo) (p1182–1183).

front: At what ejection fraction and QRS duration is cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) indicated, and how does its benefit differ from an ICD's?
back: The clearest CRT indication is symptomatic NYHA II, III or ambulatory IV HFrEF despite guideline-directed treatment, EF ≤35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB and QRS ≥150 ms. CRT can improve function and survival in selected octogenarians. An ICD prevents arrhythmic sudden death (p1184).

front: Which drug class was tested in EMPEROR-Preserved, and which outcome drove the trial's composite benefit?
back: Empagliflozin, an SGLT2 inhibitor, reduced cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization in EMPEROR-Preserved (n=5,988, EF >40%, HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.90). Fewer HF hospitalizations drove the result, irrespective of diabetes status (p1188).

front: What is the 5-year survival for older adults with established heart failure, and for patients 80 years or older specifically hospitalized with heart failure?
back: Less than 50% for older adults generally; fewer than 25% for patients ≥80y hospitalized with heart failure survive more than 5 years (p1190).

front: In a nursing-home resident, orthostatic hypotension is defined by what blood-pressure drop, and how prevalent is it in frail older nursing-home residents?
back: SBP drop ≥ 20 mmHg or DBP drop ≥ 10 mmHg on standing; up to 50% of frail nursing-home residents (p1193).

front: Name the four subtypes of orthostatic hypotension.
back: Initial (immediate, within 15 s), classic (within 3 min), delayed (>3 min), and neurogenic (autonomic-nervous-system dysfunction) (p1194).

front: What defines the cardioinhibitory type of vasovagal response, and at what age is dual-chamber pacing considered reasonable for recurrent vasovagal syncope with spontaneous pauses?
back: A cardioinhibitory vasovagal response may produce a pause ≥3 seconds or a heart rate <40/min for more than 10 seconds. Dual-chamber pacing may be reasonable in selected patients over 40 with recurrent vasovagal syncope and documented prolonged spontaneous pauses (p1194).

front: What carotid sinus massage finding defines carotid sinus hypersensitivity, and what additional feature makes it carotid sinus syndrome?
back: A pause ≥ 3 seconds or a systolic BP drop ≥ 50 mmHg during carotid sinus massage; carotid sinus syndrome requires that this be accompanied by symptoms of syncope or presyncope (p1195).

front: What proportion of permanent pacemakers are placed in patients 65 or older, and what is the leading indication in this age group?
back: More than 80%; sinoatrial (sinus node) dysfunction is the leading indication (p1193).

front: What are the highest-likelihood-to-respond criteria for cardiac resynchronization therapy?
back: LVEF ≤ 35%, sinus rhythm, LBBB, QRS ≥ 150 ms, NYHA class II, III, or ambulatory IV (p1199).

front: After TAVR, what percentage of patients develop new LBBB, and what percentage develop high-degree AV block?
back: New LBBB in 19% to 55%; high-degree AVB in 10% (p1200).

front: How many patients were randomized in the CABANA trial, and was catheter ablation superior to antiarrhythmic drugs for the primary composite endpoint?
back: 2,204 patients; catheter ablation was NOT superior to AAD for the primary endpoint (all-cause mortality, disabling stroke, serious bleeding, or cardiac arrest) at 5 years, though it did reduce AF recurrence and the combined death/cardiovascular-hospitalization secondary endpoint (p1201).

front: What CHA2DS2-VASc score threshold triggers anticoagulation in men versus women, and what is the maximum possible score?
back: ≥ 2 in men or ≥ 3 in women (p1203, Table 77-8); maximum score is 9 (p1202, Table 77-7A).

front: On the HAS-BLED score, what ranges represent low versus high bleeding risk?
back: 0–2 = low risk; 3–9 = high risk (p1202).

front: Which two DOACs show a lower major-bleeding risk than warfarin in patients 75 years or older, and which two carry an increased risk of GI bleeding at full dose?
back: Apixaban and edoxaban show lower major bleeding; full-dose dabigatran and rivaroxaban are associated with increased GI bleeding risk (p1202). Hazzard recommends a PPI with these agents. Current practice (not the book): the 2024 ESC guideline individualizes gastroprotection according to gastrointestinal bleeding risk.

front: What was the initial warfarin regimen in the original WATCHMAN studies, and what should follow-up imaging assess before changing antithrombotic therapy?
back: Hazzard gives warfarin to INR 2–3 for 45 days, then discontinues warfarin if TEE confirms complete LAA closure. Follow with aspirin and clopidogrel for 6 months, then long-term aspirin (p1203).

front: What are the primary-prevention ICD criteria for ischemic cardiomyopathy, including the required time from MI or revascularization?
back: After MI, the book gives >40 days after MI or >90 days after revascularization and, on GDMT, EF ≤35% with NYHA II–III or EF <30% with NYHA I. A separate indication after MI is NSVT with EF ≤40% and inducible sustained monomorphic VT on electrophysiologic study (p1206).

front: How is AKI classified by urine output, and which category has the best prognosis?
back: Nonoliguric (>400 mL/day), oliguric (100–400 mL/day), anuric (<100 mL/day); nonoliguric AKI has the better prognosis (p1280).

front: What proportion of older patients with acute interstitial nephritis recover partially or completely within 6 months, and what is the single most important management step?
back: About 80%; the most important step is stopping the offending drug (p1287).

front: Around what GFR does renal anemia typically develop, and what type of anemia is it?
back: Around GFR 35 mL/min; a normochromic, normocytic anemia due to inadequate erythropoietin production (p1294).

front: What two summary statistics from the National Cancer Institute establish cancer as a disease of aging?
back: Over 60% of newly diagnosed malignant tumors and 70% of all cancer deaths occur in persons 65 years or older (p1381).

front: How can loss of telomere function promote malignancy, and when has telomere shortening been measured?
back: Loss of chromosome-end protection can promote genomic instability. The chapter describes functional decline from age 30 at about 1% per year (p1383). Leukocyte measurements show that shortening is already present in early childhood and proceeds at an age-dependent rate.

front: In the New Mexico study of 800 patients over 65, what fraction were asymptomatic at cancer detection, and what fraction delayed seeking care at least 1 year?
back: Only 29% were asymptomatic at detection; 7.4% delayed seeking care for at least 1 year (p1385).

front: Does malignant melanoma present at a more or less advanced stage in older patients, and how does this compare with lung cancer?
back: Melanoma presents with more advanced-stage, deeper-penetrating local disease in older patients; lung cancer shows the opposite pattern, with older patients more often presenting with localized disease (p1385).

front: Why does breast cancer tend to behave more indolently in older women biologically, and does this translate into better overall survival?
back: Older women have a higher frequency of ER-positive tumors and longer tumor doubling times (both favorable prognostic features), but overall cancer-related survival is still lower in older women (p1385).

front: On the CARG chemotherapy-toxicity risk model, what toxicity rates correspond to the low, intermediate, and high risk-point tiers?
back: Low risk (0–5 points): 30% toxicity. Intermediate (6–9 points): 52%. High (10–19 points): 83% (p1388).

front: On the CRASH score, what hematologic and nonhematologic toxicity rates were seen in high-risk versus low-risk patients?
back: High-risk: 100% hematologic, 93% nonhematologic toxicity. Low-risk: 7% hematologic, 33% nonhematologic toxicity (p1388).

front: What T-score thresholds trigger bone-directed therapy in an older patient on aromatase-inhibitor therapy?
back: T-score less than −2.0 SD alone, OR less than −1.5 SD with one additional risk factor, OR two or more risk factors (without bone mineral density) (p1390).

front: What proportion of allogeneic HSCT recipients develop delirium, and how does historical age eligibility for allogeneic versus autologous SCT differ?
back: Up to 50% develop delirium. Allogeneic SCT was historically limited to patients under age 50, while autologous SCT has been performed in fit patients over age 70 (p1391).

front: By 2040, what proportion of US cancer survivors are projected to be 65 or older, and 75 or older?
back: 73% are projected to be 65 or older, and almost 50% are projected to be 75 or older, out of a projected 26 million total survivors (p1393).

front: חולה כשיר, נוטה למות, מסרב לאכול ולשתות. מה על הצוות לעשות ראשית?
back: לכבד את רצונו ולהימנע מטיפול רפואי בו (§15(א)); בנפרד, לעשות מאמץ סביר לשכנעו לקבל חמצן, מזון ונוזלים (אף באמצעים מלאכותיים), טיפולים שגרתיים למחלות בו-זמניות/רקע וטיפול מקל (§15(ב)).

front: חולה נוטה למות, לא-כשיר, לא בשלב סופי, "נקבע" שאינו רוצה שחייו יוארכו. מותר להימנע ממתן מזון ונוזלים?
back: לא על סמך הרצון שנקבע. סעיף 16(ב)(2) מחייב לתת טיפול נלווה, לרבות מזון ונוזלים. לפי מותב הוועדה הארצית (2016), דרך המתן נקבעת רפואית, תוך התחשבות בתועלת, בסבל ובנזק. אין חובה אוטומטית להחדיר צינור. סעיף 17 קובע דין נפרד לחולה חסר כשרות בשלב הסופי.

front: חולה בשלב סופי, לא-כשיר, "נקבע" שאינו רוצה שחייו יוארכו. מתי מותר להימנע ממתן נוזלים?
back: רק אם הרופא האחראי קבע שמתן הנוזלים עצמו גורם סבל או נזק לחולה (§17) — לא סתם על סמך "רצונו".

front: מהו ההבדל המשפטי בין §16 ל-§17?
back: §16 חל על חולה נוטה למות שאינו בשלב סופי — טיפול נלווה לעולם מוגן. §17 הוא חריג ל-§16(ב) עבור חולה בשלב סופי (בשניהם: חולה לא-כשיר, הסובל סבל משמעותי, שנקבע לגביו שאינו רוצה שחייו יוארכו) — יש להימנע (בהתאם לרצונו שנקבע) גם מטיפול נלווה, כולל מזון, אך נוזלים עדיין מוגנים — אלא אם הרופא האחראי קבע שהם גורמים סבל או נזק.

front: מטופל בגיר אינו כשיר להבין בענייניו הרפואיים, זקוק לטיפול דחוף, ואין לו מיופה כוח או אפוטרופוס. מי נותן הסכמה?
back: מקבל החלטות זמני — אדם בגיר שמאושר בכתב על ידי עובד סוציאלי במוסד הרפואי (באישור מנהל המוסד או מי שהסמיך, ובקופת חולים באישור הרופא המחוזי או מי שהסמיך), לאחר שרופא מומחה קבע שהמטופל אינו מסוגל להבין וזקוק לטיפול דחוף, לפי סדר הקדימויות בסעיף 14ב ובכפוף לחריג בסעיף 14ב(ה) למי ששמו נקוב בייפוי כוח שטרם נכנס לתוקף או בהנחיות מקדימות למינוי אפוטרופוס לפי §35א לחוק הכשרות המשפטית, בתנאי שיפעל לטובת המטופל, נתן הסכמה והצהרה בכתב והמטופל לא הביע התנגדות לאישורו (§14א(ב)(4)–(6)).

front: מהו סדר הקדימויות למקבל החלטות זמני?
back: כשאין מסמך קודם חל סדר הקדימויות: בן זוג, ילד, הורה, אח (§14ב). בני המשפחה רשאים להסכים על אדם בגיר אחר לפי התנאים שבחוק. ייפוי כוח שהופקד וטרם נכנס לתוקף, או מועמד בהנחיות מקדימות למינוי אפוטרופוס, מקנה קדימות לאדם ששמו נקבע, בכפוף לתנאי §14א.

front: כמה זמן בתוקף אישור מקבל החלטות זמני?
back: שישה חודשים מיום שניתן (§14א(ג)).

front: מטופל מינה מיופה כוח מתמשך הכולל ענייניו האישיים. יש למטופל גם בן זוג. מי מקבל החלטות רפואיות אם המטופל אינו כשיר?
back: אם ייפוי הכוח כולל סמכות רפואית ונכנס לתוקף, מיופה הכוח מחליט בגדר הסמכות שניתנה לו. אם ייפוי הכוח רק הופקד, אין לבן הזוג קדימות אוטומטית. לצורך טיפול דחוף אפשר לתת לאדם ששמו נקבע בייפוי הכוח אישור מקבל החלטות זמני לפי §§14א–14ב(ה), בכפוף לתנאים שבחוק, ולפעול במקביל להפעלת ייפוי הכוח.

front: מיופה כוח מתמשך מוסמך להחליט על אימוץ ילד של הממנה?
back: לא. מתן הסכמה למסירת ילד לאימוץ אסור באופן מוחלט על מיופה כוח, ללא יוצא מן הכלל (§32ו(ב)(3)).

front: מיופה כוח מתמשך רוצה לתת תרומה של 150,000 ש"ח בשם הממנה. מותר?
back: לא מכוח ייפוי הכוח לבדו. תרומה מותרת רק לנמען ובסכום שצוינו במפורש, ובלבד שהסכום לא יעלה במצטבר על 100,000 ש"ח (§32ו(ג)(1)(א)); תרומה מעבר לכך — גם עם הסמכה מפורשת — נדרש אישור מראש לפי §74א. הבקשה מוגשת לאפוטרופוס הכללי (§32ו(ד)(6)).

front: הממנה נתן ייפוי כוח מתמשך הכולל הסמכה להסכים לאשפוז פסיכיאטרי. במועד הבקשה בפועל, הממנה (שאינו כשיר להביע רצון מפורט) מפגין סימני התנגדות ברורים. תקפה ההסכמה?
back: לא, ככלל — הסכמת מיופה כוח לפי סעיף זה אינה תקפה אם הממנה מתנגד בעת שהתבקשה ההסכמה, אלא אם ייפוי הכוח לעניין זה נחתם גם בפני פסיכיאטר והממנה הסמיך במפורש את מיופה הכוח לתת הסכמה למרות התנגדותו; וגם אז — לא לאשפוז העולה על 48 שעות, ולא אם הממנה מסוגל באותה עת לתת הסכמה מדעת (§32ו(ג)(2)(ב)-(ד)).

front: מהו ההבדל בין "הסכמה מדעת" רגילה (§13-14) לבין הסכמה של מקבל החלטות זמני?
back: הסכמה מדעת רגילה ניתנת ישירות על ידי מטופל כשיר, לאחר גילוי מידע מלא. מקבל החלטות זמני נותן הסכמה בשם מטופל שאינו מסוגל להבין בענייניו הרפואיים, ורק לאחר שווידאו זאת (§14א(ו)).

front: מהי תוחלת החיים בלידה בישראל (2022) לנשים ולגברים?
back: נשים 84.8, גברים 80.7 שנים (ברוקדייל, שנתון 2024, עמ' 131).

front: מה דירוג ישראל עולמית בתוחלת חיים (2023), ואילו מדינות מעליה?
back: מקום 29 מתוך 236 מדינות, כ-82 שנים — אחרי מונקו (מקום 1, 86) ויפן (מקום 4, 85) (ברוקדייל, שנתון 2024, אינפוגרפיקה עמ' 35).

front: מהו הפער בשיעור המוגבלות בפעולות משק בית בין בני 65–74 לבני 75+ בקהילה?
back: 14.6% בגילי 65–74 לעומת 36.3% בבני 75+; בסך הכול 22.6% מבני 65+ (ממוצע 2020–2022) (ברוקדייל, שנתון 2024, עמ' 134).

front: מטופל בבית חולים גריאטרי מוגדר "סיעודי". מתפתח אצלו פצע לחץ דרגה 3. משנה את הסיווג?
back: כן — פצע לחץ בדרגה 3-4 הוא אחד משבעת המצבים בהגדרת "סיעודי-מורכב" (נוהל 0.2.1, §7.2), ובמטופל שכבר סיעודי באופן קבוע הוא מספיק לפי הקריאה המקובלת. שינוי הסטטוס עצמו — ע"י גריאטר המחוז לאחר ועדת הסיווג (נוהל 3.4.2, §3.5).

front: מטופל סיעודי המאושפז ב"קוד" משרד הבריאות בבי"ח גריאטרי זקוק כעת למעבר למחלקה סיעודית-מורכבת בשל צורך בהמודיאליזה סדירה. מי מחליט על שינוי הסטטוס?
back: גריאטר המחוז, לאחר החלטת ועדת הסיווג בלשכת הבריאות המחוזית הרלבנטית — לא הצוות המטפל בבית החולים לבדו (נוהל 3.4.2, §3.5 — "שינוי סטטוס" כולל מעבר לסיעוד-מורכב; הנוהל חל על מאושפזים ב"קוד". וכן, לקבלה חדשה, "סיווג" כסיעודי/תשוש נפש ע"י הגריאטר המחוזי באמצעות ועדה — נוהל 01-09 בחוזר מינהל רפואה 20/2009, §3.3).

front: מהו ההבדל בין "מטופל סיעודי" ל"מטופל סיעודי-מורכב" מבחינת ההגדרה הפורמלית?
back: "סיעודי" (§5) הוא מחלה כרונית/ליקוי קבוע הדורש מעקב רפואי מיומן לתקופה ממושכת, יחד עם ליקוי תפקודי (מרותק למיטה/עגלה, אי-שליטה בסוגרים, או מתהלך בקושי רק עקב פתולוגיה או סיבוכי מחלות). "סיעודי-מורכב" (§7) דורש בנוסף לכך גם עומס טיפולי-רפואי גבוה — לדוגמה פצע לחץ דרגה 3-4, מטופל סיעודי הזקוק בקביעות לדיאליזה, טרכאוסטומיה/BIPAP, או מחלה ממאירה הדורשת טיפול אקטיבי — המצריך צוות בעל מיומנות גבוהה יותר.

front: Can generic post-ED vulnerability scores reliably separate all high- and low-risk patients?
back: Not in the evidence reviewed here (p214). The Clinical Frailty Scale is promising for 30-day mortality, but benefit for identifying and altering return-visit or functional-decline risk remains uncertain (p217).

front: What weight-loss thresholds prompt further nutritional evaluation?
back: More than 10% over 6 months or more than 5% over 1 month before surgery; screen even patients with obesity (p373).

front: After DVT/PE, how long should elective surgery ideally wait, and when does the discussed warfarin bridging pathway apply?
back: At least 3 months. If delay is impossible, the book describes LMWH bridging while INR is <2.0, stopped 24 hours before surgery and considered again 24–48 hours afterward according to procedure, bleeding, and thrombotic risks (p380).

front: Does off-pump bypass eliminate later cognitive decline?
back: No. The chapter reports lower short-term decline (21% versus 29%) but similar decline at 6 months (31% versus 38%). Cognitive risk belongs in decisions about nonemergency surgery in patients with dementia (p380).

front: Under the chapter's EWGSOP2 approach, what comes first, what confirms muscle involvement, and what indicates severity?
back: In EWGSOP2, low strength indicates probable sarcopenia. Low muscle quantity or quality confirms it, and low physical performance indicates severity. Hazzard calls the probable stage “suspected” (p732; EWGSOP2 consensus).

front: Which domain is assessed by BIA/DXA, handgrip, and SPPB?
back: BIA/DXA estimate muscle mass; handgrip measures strength; SPPB assesses composite physical performance. The official measurement question points to p732, but the instruments are explained on p735 (p734–735).

front: What cutoff tradeoff does the book describe for SARC-F, and has screening proved cost-effective?
back: The chapter reports high sensitivity above 1 point and good specificity above 4 when comparing thresholds (p734). The usual positive SARC-F screen is 4/10 or higher (p771). Screening cost-effectiveness has not been established.

front: Give the EWGSOP2 grip and gait thresholds, and explain the SDOC gait footnote.
back: Grip <27 kg in men and <16 kg in women; gait ≤0.8 m/s. The table also displays ≤0.8 m/s for SDOC but explicitly says SDOC has no precise cutoff and this value derives from the earlier FNIH consensus (Table 49-4, p735).

front: What may cause low grip strength other than sarcopenia, and why still act on the finding?
back: Hand osteoarthritis, low motivation, and neurologic disorders are examples. Low grip predicts adverse outcomes regardless of cause, so intervention is justified even if additional tests are unavailable (p735).

front: What does SPPB add to gait speed, and what can replace a dynamometer when needed?
back: SPPB adds balance and sit-to-stand performance reflecting strength/power/endurance. Sit-to-stand can also serve as a strength proxy without a dynamometer; TUG is a physical-performance test (p735–736).

front: How do cachexia and physical frailty overlap with, but differ from, sarcopenia?
back: Cachexia is severe weight loss/wasting in disease with excess catabolism and inflammation and may coexist with sarcopenia. Frailty overlaps through weight loss, weakness, and slowness, but can arise from nonmuscular disease; mild sarcopenia need not cause frailty (p736).

front: What protein targets does the chapter give for healthy older adults and those with disease?
back: 1–1.2 g/kg/day in healthy older adults; up to 1.5 g/kg/day with disease, compared with the former 0.8 g/kg/day recommendation. Consider high-protein oral supplements when usual food cannot meet the target (p737).

front: What limits the conclusions about HMB/leucine and vitamin D?
back: HMB/leucine usually appeared within complete supplements; isolated effects and optimal candidates remain uncertain. Vitamin D has not improved function in sarcopenic patients overall, though severe deficiency may be a responsive setting (p737).

front: Which functional changes are clinically relevant when assessing treatment?
back: Gait-speed improvement >0.1 m/s or SPPB improvement >1 point. Mass gain alone is insufficient; mobility, daily activities, falls, fatigue, and quality of life matter to patients (p738).

front: Which node has the greatest pacemaker-cell loss, and why must its quoted percentage be qualified?
back: The SA node. Table 73-1 gives 75% loss (p1116), whereas the narrative gives 90% by age 70 (p1117). AV nodal losses are more modest; the figures should not be transferred to the AV node.

front: What happens to SR calcium storage and release between beats?
back: Accumulation, retention, and effective reuptake decrease; spontaneous leak increases, leaving less calcium available for the next contraction and slowing relaxation. The almost 50% reduction in reuptake is from old rat/mouse hearts; reduced SERCA content is also described in humans. (p1117)

front: How does age-associated fibrosis differ from an infarct scar?
back: Increased interstitial collagen creates a diffuse delicate pattern rather than focal post-infarction scar patches. Ischemia and hypertension can accelerate it but are not required; human imaging studies of healthy aging are not uniform. (p1117)

front: Does common amyloid deposition in very old hearts rule out clinically significant amyloid cardiomyopathy?
back: No. Deposition may increase diastolic stiffness, and in some patients the burden causes progressive heart failure. Systemic senile amyloidosis is much less common than atrium-restricted deposition. (p1117)

front: What is the chapter's synthesis of indexed LV mass and LA size with healthy aging?
back: LV mass usually shows no change to a slight reduction after body-size adjustment, while LA size commonly increases. LA size alone does not identify the cause of chronically raised filling pressure. (p1118)

front: What distinguishes coronary atherosclerosis from Mönckeberg medial calcification in this chapter?
back: Atherosclerosis is disease; medial calcification is described as probably age-related degeneration. Aging also brings coronary dilation and tortuosity. (p1120)

front: State the directions of change in PR/QRS/QT, LV relaxation, and aortic impedance.
back: PR/QRS/QT lengthen; LV stiffness increases and relaxation decreases; aortic impedance increases as arteries stiffen. (Table 73-2, p1121)

front: How do resting and maximum exercise heart rate differ with healthy aging?
back: Resting rate is generally unchanged, while maximum exercise rate declines. The book's prediction for healthy adults is 208 − (0.7 × age). (p1121)

front: Can a restrictive filling pattern or new regional wall-motion abnormality be dismissed as normal aging?
back: No. Expected delayed relaxation should be interpreted against age norms; restrictive/pseudonormal filling suggests disease (p1123). Regional wall-motion abnormalities remain abnormal (p1124, p1127).

front: What are the book's CKD duration requirement and stage subdivisions for moderately reduced GFR?
back: Kidney damage or reduced function for at least 3 months. Stage 3 spans 30–59 mL/min/1.73 m²: 3A is 45–59 and 3B is 30–44 (p1269).

front: Why does measured creatinine clearance overestimate GFR, and what marker avoids reduced creatinine production?
back: Some urinary creatinine is secreted by proximal tubules rather than filtered. Cystatin C avoids the age-related creatinine-production problem (p1269).

front: What does calcium accomplish in severe hyperkalemia, and which treatment removes potassium rather than merely shifting it?
back: Calcium stabilizes the myocardial membrane without lowering potassium. Insulin, beta-agonists, and bicarbonate in metabolic acidosis shift potassium into cells; loop-diuretic-driven excretion, exchange resins, and dialysis remove it (p1271).

front: Is nonsurgical care excluded for every hip fracture?
back: No. It may be considered for selected patients, including those with very high surgical risk, very short life expectancy, or advanced dementia with contractures; prior function and goals matter. (p. 797)

front: What nonmedical factors can determine safe discharge home?
back: Home layout, social support, caregiver availability and resources, alongside mobility and self-care ability; a home assessment by therapy staff supplies essential information. (p. 798)

front: What distinguishes primary from specialist palliative care?
back: All clinicians can provide core symptom management, coordination, goals discussions and caregiver support; specialists contribute an interprofessional team with palliative expertise. (p. 1045)

front: What did the noncancer palliative-care meta-analysis associate with palliative care?
back: Less emergency department use, hospitalization and symptom burden; dementia trials had been least promising. (p. 1047)

front: What should precede medication for dementia-related behavioral symptoms?
back: Identify the behavior and severity, identify and remove physiologic/environmental triggers when possible, and attempt nonpharmacologic interventions. (p. 1047)

front: What pain-treatment approach reduced behavioral symptoms in a nursing-home trial?
back: An empiric stepwise protocol; most patients received acetaminophen at the first step. Opioids may be tried for nonresponders, and PAINAD may help assessment. (p. 1048)

front: What domains structure care for multimorbidity?
back: Patient preferences, interpretation of evidence, prognosis, clinical feasibility, and optimization of therapies/care plans. (p. 1049)

front: Why are age-specific cancer treatment estimates uncertain?
back: Older adults are underrepresented in trials; function, comorbidities, treatment toxicity and social support must be considered when applying the evidence. (p1435)

front: What CRC presentation differences are described in older adults?
back: More right-sided tumors, obstruction and perforation, with a greater likelihood of acute presentation; stage distribution is similar to younger adults. (p. 1437)

front: Why can overall and cancer-specific survival tell different stories?
back: Comorbid diseases account for substantial mortality; some investigators found age-related overall-survival differences were no longer significant after excluding noncancer deaths. (p1438)

front: What limitation of sigmoidoscopy matters particularly in older adults?
back: It misses proximal tumors beyond its reach, and older adults are more likely to have proximal neoplasia. (p1439)

front: What time horizon helps frame stopping CRC screening?
back: Stopping may be reasonable when life expectancy is shorter than the 5-10 years for a polyp to progress to cancer. (p1440)

front: What minimum lymph-node count defines adequate evaluation in the CRC surgical analysis?
back: At least 12 lymph nodes; inadequate evaluation correlated with inferior survival. (p1440)

front: Is oxaliplatin's adjuvant survival benefit established equally in all older adults?
back: No. Older-subgroup findings are mixed, with several showing no added survival advantage; it can be considered for fit adults with minimal comorbidity. (p1441)

front: Which oxaliplatin toxicity can undermine function and increase falls?
back: Peripheral neuropathy. (p1441)

front: What pancreatic-cancer diagnostic shortcut can incorrectly assign a poor prognosis?
back: Omitting accurate tissue confirmation to spare diagnostic discomfort; older patients receive pathological confirmation less frequently and may be misdiagnosed. (p1445)

front: What is the potentially curative treatment for localized pancreatic cancer?
back: Surgical resection; it can be safe in carefully selected older adults. (p1445)

front: Which rare serious toxicity is described for gemcitabine?
back: Hemolytic uremic syndrome; liver-enzyme elevations are also described. (p1445)

front: Which patients received olaparib maintenance in POLO, and at what dose?
back: Patients with germline BRCA-mutated metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma without progression after at least 16 weeks of continuous first-line platinum-based chemotherapy; olaparib 300 mg twice daily. (p. 1446)

front: Did POLO's progression-free benefit establish an overall-survival benefit in its interim analysis?
back: No. Progression-free survival improved, while interim overall survival did not differ. (p1446)

front: What symptom-directed interventions are described for pancreatic cancer?
back: Biliary stents or percutaneous drainage for obstruction, microencapsulated lipase for pancreatic insufficiency, and possible celiac plexus neurolysis for pain. (p. 1446)

front: Does the chapter describe age as an absolute exclusion from esophageal surgery?
back: No. Most, but not all, studies suggest age is not limiting; the evidence includes contradictory morbidity and mortality findings, so assess individual fitness and comorbidities. (p1449)

front: Which patients with MDS are more likely to benefit from erythropoietin?
back: Those with lower-risk scores, serum erythropoietin <500 mU/mL, low transfusion requirements and a shorter interval from diagnosis to treatment. (p. 1485)

front: What is the lenalidomide-responsive cytogenetic MDS subset, and what cautions matter?
back: Transfusion-dependent disease with deletion of the long arm of chromosome 5 as the sole abnormality; watch myelosuppression and adjust dosing for renal impairment. (p. 1486)

front: What is critical for successful oral TKI treatment of CML?
back: Daily adherence and careful response monitoring; PCR provides sensitive monitoring, and comorbid cardiac/thrombotic risks inform drug selection. (p. 1490)

front: What BTK-inhibitor risks matter in an anticoagulated patient with CLL?
back: Increased bleeding risk, plus cardiovascular toxicities such as atrial fibrillation, heart failure and hypertension. (p. 1491)

front: How should new anemia in CLL be evaluated for hemolysis?
back: Reticulocyte count and direct Coombs testing help distinguish hemolysis from decreased marrow production. (p. 1492)

front: How do renal dosing requirements differ for lenalidomide and bortezomib?
back: Lenalidomide requires dose adjustment for renal insufficiency; bortezomib does not. (p. 1505)

front: Does pyuria convert asymptomatic bacteriuria into symptomatic UTI?
back: No. ASB can occur with or without pyuria in the absence of localizing genitourinary symptoms. (p1699)

front: What distinguishes simple cystitis from complicated UTI in this chapter?
back: Simple cystitis is confined to the bladder; complicated infection extends beyond it, including renal-parenchymal infection in pyelonephritis. (p1700)

front: How is recurrent UTI defined?
back: At least 3 symptomatic UTIs in 12 months or 2 in 6 months, following clinical resolution of each episode with treatment. (p. 1700)

front: Does a high postvoid residual consistently predict symptomatic UTI?
back: No. Study findings conflict; high residuals were not consistently associated with symptomatic infection in ambulatory women or long-term-care residents. (p1702)

front: What are the different purposes of McGeer and Loeb criteria?
back: Original/revised McGeer criteria support nursing-home surveillance; Loeb minimum criteria support clinical antibiotic decisions. (p. 1705)

front: What belongs in active monitoring for nonspecific symptoms?
back: Frequent vital-sign, hydration and symptom checks; hydration support; alternative-diagnosis assessment; and explicit criteria for notifying the physician about deterioration or persistence. (p. 1705)

front: What TMP/SMX regimen and local-resistance cutoff are given?
back: 160/800 mg twice daily for 3 days for simple cystitis; avoid empiric use if local uropathogen resistance exceeds 20%. (p. 1708)

front: Which important TMP/SMX interactions should be recognized?
back: Warfarin, with increased INR, and sulfonylureas, with increased hypoglycemia risk. (p. 1709)

front: What is the fosfomycin dose and its usual place in simple-cystitis treatment?
back: 3 g as a single oral dose; generally reserved for highly resistant pathogens or inability to use other first-line agents. It is not recommended for complicated UTI. (p. 1709)

front: Can an older man have simple cystitis?
back: Yes. Men should not automatically be classified as having complicated UTI, but require careful assessment for infection extending beyond the bladder. (p1710)

front: When may a week of antibiotics suffice for an older man with simple cystitis?
back: For most, 7 days is adequate if the response is prompt, within 72 hours. (p1711)

front: What warning signs prevent a nonspecific presentation from being treated as routine observation alone?
back: Fever, rigors/chills, unstable vital signs or new clear-cut delirium warrant evaluation for infection and noninfectious causes; assess whether the presentation is consistent with UTI. (p. 1712)

front: What question can reveal preclinical mobility limitation in an independent patient?
back: Ask whether the patient has changed how they walk longer distances or climb stairs, even if they still complete those activities. (p743)

front: Which tasks make up the SPPB?
back: Timed four-meter walk, five chair rises and three standing balance challenges. (p743)

front: How do you interpret an SPPB score below ten?
back: It identifies risk of disability. A one-point change is considered substantial in the table. (p743)

front: What does the Timed Up and Go include besides walking?
back: Rising from the chair, turning after walking ten feet, returning to the chair and sitting down. (p744)

front: What does a TUG between twenty and thirty seconds suggest?
back: The time is slower than the book's community-mobility benchmark but does not reach its greater-than-thirty-second assistance benchmark. Assess the tasks that were difficult. (p744)

front: Which distance changes are meaningful on the six-minute walk?
back: The table describes 20 m as a small meaningful change and 50 m as substantial. (p744)

front: How is the long-distance corridor walk scored?
back: Record distance in the first two minutes and then the time to complete 400 m. Slower completion is associated with later disability. (p744)

front: Why record walking instructions and starting method?
back: Standing and rolling starts and different instructions can affect measured speed. Repeat the same protocol when following change. (p744–745)

front: How does a stride differ from a step?
back: A step runs between consecutive opposite-foot contacts. A stride spans successive contacts of the same foot. (p747–748)

front: How does double support change with age?
back: A greater proportion of the gait cycle is spent with both feet on the ground. Gait speed and step length tend to decrease. (p747)

front: Why can an adequate clinic walk coexist with restricted activity at home?
back: The test measures performance under defined conditions. The home environment, available support and daily behavior influence actual mobility. (p745, p749–750)

front: What should be observed first when the patient arrives in a wheelchair?
back: Assess bed and chair movement and whether standing or walking is possible with assistance. Select subsequent tasks accordingly. (p751–752)

front: What can reveal difficulty when usual walking appears normal?
back: Single-leg stance, tandem walking, longer distances or complex tasks such as obstacles, turns and walking while doing another task. (p751–752)

front: Why can too much help worsen mobility?
back: Assistance that replaces a task the patient can perform reduces practice. Repeated disuse can contribute to weakness and loss of function. (p750)

front: What should accompany treatment of an identified gait impairment?
back: Practice the relevant task and address strength, balance, endurance and flexibility. Adapt the environment or walking aid to the patient's goals and limitations. (p755)

front: How can cueing help distinguish retrieval from storage failure?
back: Improvement with cues or recognition supports a retrieval problem. Poor recall despite cues favors impaired storage. (p139, p141)

front: What does a positive Hoover test show?
back: Voluntary hip extension appears weak, but involuntary extension is present when the opposite hip flexes against resistance, supporting functional weakness. (p146)

front: Which laboratory pattern suggests an intrinsic-pathway problem?
back: A prolonged aPTT with normal PT. Consider heparin exposure, factor deficiency or a circulating inhibitor, then use the bleeding history to narrow the possibilities. (p1512–1513)

front: Which factor deficiency can first present with excessive surgical or dental bleeding?
back: Factor XI deficiency can cause a variable bleeding history with few spontaneous events. (p1512–1513)

front: What isolated PT abnormality can arise with inadequate nutrition?
back: Vitamin K deficiency can prolong PT before the aPTT becomes abnormal. (p1512–1513)

front: Why can a lupus anticoagulant confound the interpretation of a prolonged aPTT?
back: It prolongs a laboratory clotting time while clinically being associated with thrombosis. (p1512–1513)

front: What warrants evaluating for acquired factor VIII inhibition?
back: New spontaneous skin, muscle or GI bleeding in an older adult without a prior bleeding history, particularly with a prolonged aPTT. (p1512)

front: How does drug-induced thrombocytopenia within hours differ from a fall several days later?
back: Preexisting antibodies can produce a fall within 24 hours. An anamnestic immune response typically occurs at 3–10 days in Figure 96-3. (p1514)

front: Which complication should be sought when platelets fall during heparin therapy?
back: Arterial or venous thrombosis. Use the clinical 4T score and appropriate laboratory testing to assess HIT. (p1514–1515)

front: When does the book discuss initial corticosteroids for primary ITP?
back: For newly diagnosed primary ITP, platelets below 30 × 10⁹/L and no or minor mucocutaneous bleeding. Monitor glucose, blood pressure and other steroid toxicity. (p1514)

front: What do recurrent strokes with thrombocytopenia suggest?
back: Consider antiphospholipid syndrome. An initial positive antibody test should be repeated at least 12 weeks later to establish persistence. (p1516)

front: Which conditions in a thrombosis history imply an acquired hypercoagulable state?
back: Examples include malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, antiphospholipid syndrome, HIT and myeloproliferative neoplasms. (p1515–1516)

front: How can age complicate D-dimer interpretation?
back: Aging, acute inflammation, surgery and malignancy can elevate D-dimer without an acute VTE, reducing specificity. (p1517)

front: What age-adjusted D-dimer threshold does the book describe for suspected PE?
back: Age in years × 10 µg/L in outpatients aged 50 or over when the assay uses a conventional cutoff of 500 µg/L, interpreted with clinical probability. (p1519)

front: When might V/Q scanning help evaluate suspected PE?
back: When contrast allergy or severe renal insufficiency makes CTPA unsuitable. A normal chest radiograph makes the scan easier to interpret. (p1519)

front: What overlap is required when warfarin starts for acute VTE?
back: Continue parenteral anticoagulation for at least 5 days and until the INR has been above 2.0 for at least 24 hours. (p1520)

front: What medication changes may reduce bleeding during anticoagulation?
back: Review the need for antiplatelet therapy and NSAIDs. Remove unnecessary antiplatelet treatment and consider an alternative analgesic where appropriate. (p1522)

front: What distinguishes short-stay from long-stay goals?
back: After an acute illness, stabilization and recovery of sufficient function to return home may be realistic. Long-stay care often emphasizes maintaining abilities, comfort and quality of life (p224, p227).

front: Who may detect an important change before the clinician sees the resident?
back: Direct-care staff who know the resident's usual mobility, intake and behavior. Include their observations in the assessment (p221, p223).

front: What makes an interdisciplinary plan actionable?
back: Specify the problem, the goal agreed with the resident, the intervention, the responsible team members and a review date (p225).

front: Why document function on entry as well as diagnoses?
back: A baseline allows the team to distinguish established impairments from relocation effects or a new and potentially reversible decline (p226).

front: When does the US assessment schedule described here require a new comprehensive MDS?
back: At admission, after a major change and annually, with selected sections updated quarterly (p226).

front: What should a pharmacist check in the transferred medication list?
back: Reconcile the list and check indications, interactions with other drugs or diseases, stop dates and the planned monitoring (p227).

front: Which nutrition intervention may be missed when weight falls?
back: Review intake, food preferences and whether a restrictive diet is both unnecessary and unappetizing (p227).

front: What is a reasonable therapy goal when further gains are unlikely?
back: Preserve current abilities. Environmental changes may support function or allow discharge even when recovery is limited (p227).

front: What proportion of people admitted from hospital are readmitted within a month in the chapter's figures?
back: About one in five within 30 days (p230).

front: Why can a hospital transfer permanently alter baseline function?
back: Bed rest can cause deconditioning and loss of transfer or walking ability. Delirium, devices, infection and pressure injuries can compound the decline (p230).

front: What does INTERACT add when an acute illness develops?
back: Early recognition and a structured on-site assessment, timely treatment when feasible, and prompt transfer when the resident needs hospital resources (p230, p233).

front: What drainage method did the exam select for a neurogenic bladder after paraplegia?
back: Intermittent catheterization when practical. It avoids continuous exposure to an indwelling catheter (Chapter 47, p715–716; see p232).

front: Should chronic catheter use itself trigger continuous antibiotic prophylaxis?
back: No. The prophylaxis row specifically advises against continuous antibiotics in chronically catheterized residents (p232).

front: Why discuss goals before an acute illness?
back: Advance planning allows the resident or proxy to consider whether treatment on site, hospitalization or comfort care fits the resident's preferences and likely benefit (p232–234).

front: Where does autonomy enter routine long-term care?
back: Residents with capacity may choose daily routines and voice preferences about care. When capacity is impaired, involve the appropriate surrogate and continue to attend to the resident's wishes (p234).

front: How can an older patient appear normal at rest despite poor physiological reserve?
back: Homeostenosis narrows the range within which a physiological system can compensate for stress. A disturbance may reveal a deficit hidden at baseline. (p575–576, p580)

front: Which cold responses can be impaired after prolonged immobilization?
back: Cold perception, shivering intensity, thermogenesis and peripheral vasoconstriction can all decline with aging. (p581–582)

front: How does the book define hypothermia for clinical purposes?
back: Core temperature below 35°C, measured with a suitable tympanic, rectal or esophageal probe. (p582)

front: Why can indoor settings still pose a hypothermia risk?
back: An immobile or frail patient may not notice cold or generate enough heat, even in an air-conditioned facility. (p582–583)

front: Which reversible causes should be considered in unexplained hypothermia?
back: Assess for infection, hypoglycemia, hypothyroidism, malnutrition, sedating drugs and prolonged immobility. (p583)

front: Which ECG feature can support hypothermia?
back: J or Osborne waves after the QRS are relatively specific and can disappear as temperature returns toward normal. (p583)

front: What makes severe hypothermia a cardiac emergency?
back: Bradycardia and ventricular dysrhythmias can occur, and even minor stimulation may precipitate arrhythmia. Cardiac monitoring is important. (p583)

front: Which responses to heat may be impaired?
back: Sweating, cutaneous vasodilatation and the ability to raise cardiac output can diminish, limiting heat loss. (p581, p584–585)

front: Why does an absence of thirst fail to exclude significant dehydration?
back: Thirst perception diminishes with age, and the kidney may be less able to conserve water and sodium during depletion. (p581, p586)

front: How does vasopressin respond to osmotic versus volume stress?
back: The response to hyperosmotic stimuli can increase, while the response to hypovolemia may be impaired. (p581, p586)

front: What determines how symptomatic hyponatremia appears?
back: Both the magnitude and speed of the sodium fall matter. Interpret mental-status change against the patient's usual cognition. (p586–587)

front: Which fluid does the book use first for hypernatremia with shock?
back: Start 0.9% saline to restore effective circulation, then address the water deficit with more hypotonic fluid. (p588)

front: Why can a high BUN-to-creatinine ratio mislead?
back: Low muscle mass can lower creatinine and raise the ratio. Low protein intake can also obscure the expected BUN rise. (p589)

front: What endocrine disorder can present as repeated saline-responsive hypotension?
back: Consider adrenal or isolated mineralocorticoid deficiency. The absence of frank hyperkalemia does not exclude it. (p589)

front: Why can medication for urgency precipitate urinary retention?
back: Aging or obstruction may reduce detrusor contractile reserve. An anticholinergic can push an underactive bladder into retention. (p589–590)

front: Which drug class in the refractory-heartburn question reduces LES pressure?
back: Calcium-channel blockers, represented by amlodipine. A PPI suppresses acid production but does not restore sphincter tone (p1316).

front: Where do aspirin, ibuprofen and prednisone appear in the drug table?
back: In the direct mucosal-injury group. The question asks about reduced sphincter pressure (p1316).

front: Which other drugs can promote reflux by reducing LES pressure?
back: Examples include nitrates, theophylline, benzodiazepines, dopaminergic agents, tricyclic antidepressants and anticholinergics (p1316).

front: Which symptoms can overshadow heartburn in older people with esophagitis?
back: Dysphagia, loss of appetite, anemia and weight loss. Symptom intensity can underestimate mucosal injury (p1317–1318).

front: What can endoscopy show that a symptomatic response to a PPI cannot?
back: The severity of mucosal injury and structural complications such as a peptic stricture or Barrett esophagus (p1317).

front: When does a barium examination add information?
back: When a ring, structural narrowing, impaired motility or a swallowing disorder is suspected. Videofluoroscopy can characterize swallowing (p1317).

front: What practical advice reduces pill contact with the esophageal mucosa?
back: Swallow potentially injurious medicines with a full glass of water while upright, and review whether the drug is needed (p1318).

front: Which agents were most effective at healing erosive esophagitis in the trials summarized?
back: PPIs outperformed H2 antagonists. Studied daily doses include omeprazole 20 mg and pantoprazole 40 mg (p1319).

front: Which factors can conceal H. pylori during testing?
back: Recent antibiotics or acid suppression and gastric atrophy can lower test sensitivity. Consider which part of the stomach was biopsied (p1327).

front: Why choose a breath or fecal antigen test over antibody testing to check eradication?
back: The former assess ongoing infection. Antibody testing has poorer accuracy for this purpose. The book advises waiting at least a month after therapy (p1327).

front: How may upper GI bleeding present without obvious hematemesis?
back: Melena, hematochezia with acute bleeding, or occult blood loss presenting as anemia (p1331).

front: What is assessed immediately when bleeding is suspected?
back: Hemodynamic status and need for resuscitation, followed by bleeding history, drug exposures, blood count and coagulation studies (p1332–1333).

front: Does a history of cirrhosis establish variceal bleeding?
back: No. In the chapter, more than half of upper GI bleeds in cirrhosis arise from nonvariceal sources (p1332).

front: What benefit does the book attribute to high-dose IV PPI before endoscopy?
back: It may reduce the need for endoscopic hemostasis, without a demonstrated improvement in final clinical outcomes (p1333).

front: What links autoimmune atrophic gastritis to pernicious anemia?
back: Loss of corpus/fundus parietal-cell function reduces acid and intrinsic-factor production. Histology of the involved mucosa supports the diagnosis (p1335).

front: How does the typical distribution of myofascial pain differ from fibromyalgia?
back: Myofascial pain is often regional, with a trigger point in a taut band. Fibromyalgia produces widespread pain. The disorders can coexist. (p1643–1644, p1654)

front: What symptoms should accompany the pain history in suspected fibromyalgia?
back: Ask about fatigue, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive symptoms, mood and the effect of symptoms on function. (p1643–1645)

front: Does a positive fibromyalgia screening score establish the diagnosis?
back: No. Interpret it alongside a history, examination and assessment for other treatable explanations or comorbid disease. (p1643–1646)

front: Which alteration in sleep architecture occurs in fibromyalgia?
back: The book describes REM deficiency and alpha-wave intrusion into slow-wave sleep, with frequent awakenings and less total sleep. (p1649)

front: What treatable sleep disorders deserve consideration?
back: Sleep apnea, restless legs syndrome and periodic limb movement disorder. Use diagnostic polysomnography where indicated. (p1649)

front: Why examine the joints and soft tissues even when the pain is widespread?
back: Synovitis or extrasynovial signs can point to rheumatic disease that warrants evaluation and may coexist with fibromyalgia. (p1646)

front: What accompanies a medication trial in fibromyalgia?
back: Education, individualized activity and aerobic exercise. Psychological or interdisciplinary approaches may also improve pain and function. (p1647, p1653–1654)

front: How do the authors start duloxetine in an older adult?
back: Start at 20 mg daily and increase slowly toward 60 mg over at least several weeks if tolerated. Monitor blood pressure and orthostatic symptoms. (p1649)

front: Why might an SNRI be chosen before a tricyclic antidepressant?
back: The authors cite a lower burden of adverse effects. This preference when choosing a drug does not define a universal first treatment for fibromyalgia. (p1647)

front: How should duloxetine be stopped according to the chapter?
back: Taper gradually, reducing by no more than 50% at intervals of one to two weeks to reduce withdrawal symptoms. (p1649)

front: Why start a gabapentinoid cautiously?
back: Sedation and dizziness can impair balance. Titrate gradually and consider renal function. (p1649, p1653)

front: What finding supports a myofascial trigger point?
back: A palpable nodule in a taut muscle band that reproduces the usual local or referred pain. Pressure may also elicit a local twitch. (p1654, p1656–1658)

front: Why might myofascial pain resemble radiculopathy?
back: It can refer pain outside the muscle and produce burning or paresthesias. Examine for a reproducible trigger point and neurologic findings. (p1643, p1656–1658)

front: What perpetuating factors should be sought before repeating local treatment?
back: Consider abnormal mechanics, limited joint motion, postural strain, muscle weakness or a leg-length discrepancy. (p1657–1659)

front: Which approach does the chapter emphasize for myofascial functional recovery?
back: Stretching, local treatment and correction of perpetuating factors, alongside education and activity. Medication alone usually does not restore function. (p1664)

front: Why might HIV diagnosis be delayed in an older person?
back: Symptoms such as fatigue, weight loss or anemia can be attributed to other illnesses, and clinicians or patients may underestimate exposure risk. (p1719–1720)

front: What findings can prompt diagnostic HIV testing independent of routine screening age?
back: Examples include unexplained cytopenias, oral candidiasis, neuropathy, recurrent pneumonia or another HIV-associated illness. (p1720)

front: Should treatment wait for CD4 decline in newly diagnosed HIV?
back: The book recommends ART regardless of count and prompt linkage to care. Older adults may have slower CD4 recovery despite virologic suppression. (p1720–1721)

front: What factors influence ART selection in an older adult?
back: Consider comorbidities, existing organ injury, concomitant medications, likely resistance, patient preference and cost. (p1721)

front: How do accelerated and accentuated comorbidity differ?
back: Accelerated describes earlier onset. Accentuated describes higher prevalence compared with peers. Both influence screening and follow-up. (p1721)

front: What causes shingles decades after chickenpox?
back: Reactivation of a person's latent varicella-zoster virus. Aging and impaired cellular immunity increase risk. (p1725)

front: Which autoimmune disease is explicitly listed among zoster risk conditions?
back: Systemic lupus erythematosus. Transplant, hematologic malignancy, HIV and immunosuppressive medicines are additional settings. (p1725)

front: How can zoster mimic a noncutaneous disease?
back: Dermatomal pain or hypersensitivity can precede visible lesions and mimic visceral, cardiac or neurologic pain. Zoster sine herpete can occur without rash. (p1726)

front: When might the clinical appearance alone be insufficient?
back: An atypical eruption, suspected organ involvement or a need to distinguish recurrent HSV from zoster can justify confirmatory testing. (p1727)

front: What defines postherpetic neuralgia in this chapter?
back: Pain persisting at least 90 days after onset of the rash. (p1725)

front: What should prompt ophthalmology involvement?
back: Ophthalmic zoster with ocular symptoms or findings, including painful visual change, because corneal and intraocular inflammation can threaten sight. (p1726–1728)

front: Can ocular involvement still warrant antiviral treatment after three days?
back: Yes. Ophthalmic zoster and continuing new vesicles are exceptions to the trial-based 72-hour window. (p1727–1728)

front: What acyclovir regimen is listed for immunocompetent adults with cranial nerve involvement?
back: Oral acyclovir 800 mg five times a day for seven days, with renal adjustment. Oral valacyclovir or famciclovir are less frequent alternatives. (p1727)

front: Why avoid routine corticosteroids for zoster?
back: They have not prevented postherpetic neuralgia in trials and may cause harm. If used for selected acute indications, they accompany antiviral therapy. (p1728)

front: What should patients expect after recombinant vaccination?
back: Local pain and systemic symptoms may occur. Serious adverse events were similar between vaccine and placebo groups in clinical trials. (p1728–1729)

front: When does a presumed actinic keratosis require biopsy?
back: When it is thick or indurated, remains suspicious or fails appropriate treatment. The concern is underlying keratinocyte carcinoma. (p1457)

front: What is the usual clinical appearance of nodular BCC?
back: A shiny or pearly papule or nodule, often with branching surface vessels and a rolled border. (p1457)

front: Why reassess a persistent eczema-like plaque?
back: Superficial BCC can resemble an inflammatory rash and may be overlooked if treatment is repeatedly continued without reassessment. (p1458)

front: Which appearance should raise concern for cutaneous SCC?
back: A firm hyperkeratotic pink or red papule, nodule or plaque, sometimes tender, bleeding or ulcerated. (p1459–1460)

front: Why might a crateriform lesion that grows over weeks be excised?
back: Keratoacanthomas may regress, but their behavior is difficult to predict and they resemble other SCCs. (p1459)

front: What makes an eyelid BCC or a recurrent BCC clinically important?
back: Both are higher-risk features for subclinical extension or recurrence and affect selection of a margin-controlled treatment. (p1460–1462)

front: When is systemic vismodegib relevant?
back: For metastatic or locally advanced inoperable BCC when usual local approaches are unsuitable. Site and recurrence prompt careful assessment of these conditions. (p1462)

front: What toxicities can limit hedgehog inhibitors?
back: Muscle spasms, dysgeusia and weight loss are important examples. Monitor functional and nutritional consequences. (p1463)

front: What do the topical fluorouracil and imiquimod regimens on p1461 treat?
back: They describe actinic keratosis. Selected biopsy-confirmed low-risk superficial BCC can also be treated topically, with a different regimen. (p1461)

front: What does melanoma asymmetry mean at the bedside?
back: The two halves are not mirror images. Examine border irregularity, variation in color and change over time as well. (p1464)

front: Can a small changing pigmented lesion be melanoma?
back: Yes. Diameter alone is insensitive. Evolution, darkness and difference from the patient's other nevi may identify a concerning lesion. (p1464)

front: Why avoid a superficial sampling shave in suspected melanoma?
back: It may transect the lesion and prevent accurate determination of Breslow depth. The book describes complete full-thickness excision or deep saucerization. (p1467)

front: Why coordinate sentinel-node biopsy with definitive excision when indicated?
back: Node assessment provides staging information and is ideally planned with definitive surgery to preserve mapping of the primary lesion's drainage. (p1467–1468)

front: What distinguishes invasive SCC from BCC in metastatic behavior?
back: Regional nodal metastasis is more common with SCC. BCC can still cause major local damage despite rarely metastasizing. (p1458, p1460–1462)

front: When might palliative surgery be worthwhile near the end of life?
back: When a painful, bleeding or malodorous lesion substantially affects comfort, even if observation would be appropriate for asymptomatic low-risk disease. (p1471)

front: Why can a relatively benign abdominal examination be misleading?
back: Visceral sensation can decline with aging. Serious ischemia or perforation may produce little tenderness. (p1299, p1302)

front: Which bowel preparation risk is especially important in an older adult?
back: Sodium phosphate can cause electrolyte disturbance, fluid shifts and phosphate nephropathy. Polyethylene glycol is generally well tolerated. (p1302)

front: What is distinctive about diverticular hemorrhage?
back: Often brisk and painless. Although diverticula predominate on the left, bleeding frequently originates in the right colon. (p1303)

front: How should a positive C. difficile PCR be interpreted?
back: It may identify an asymptomatic carrier. Interpret it in a patient with compatible diarrhea and review precipitating antibiotic exposure. (p1304–1305)

front: Why is IV vancomycin inappropriate treatment for C. difficile colitis?
back: It does not attain adequate colonic luminal concentrations. The chapter's vancomycin regimen for initial mild–moderate illness is oral. (p1305)

front: What suggests microscopic colitis despite a normal colonoscopy?
back: Chronic watery diarrhea, often with an unremarkable examination. Exclude infection and obtain biopsies to establish the histologic diagnosis. (p1305–1306)

front: Which steroid is used to induce remission in microscopic colitis?
back: Oral budesonide 9 mg daily. Its relatively low systemic absorption is valuable in an older adult. (p1306)

front: What influences colorectal cancer risk in long-standing IBD?
back: Duration, extent and degree of colonic inflammation. Crohn colitis may carry a risk similar to UC. (p1309)

front: When does the book begin surveillance in long-standing colonic IBD?
back: Eight to ten years after onset, with colonoscopy and biopsies every one to three years. Consider continued rectal surveillance after subtotal colectomy. (p1309)

front: How can chronic small-bowel ischemia present?
back: Meal-related abdominal pain may lead to food avoidance and weight loss. (p1309)

front: Which setting should raise suspicion for Ogilvie syndrome?
back: New abdominal distention during severe illness or following abdominal, pelvic, hip or knee surgery, often with failure to pass flatus or stool. (p1310)

front: Why pay particular attention to the cecal diameter?
back: The cecum usually has the largest radius and therefore high wall tension with dilation. A diameter of at least 12 cm meets the chapter's definition of megacolon. (p1310)

front: What reversible causes should be addressed in acute pseudo-obstruction?
back: Correct electrolyte disturbances, hypovolemia and hypoxemia. Review motility-impairing medications and provide hydration and bowel rest. (p1311)

front: What must be excluded before neostigmine is considered?
back: Mechanical obstruction. Review contraindications such as bradycardia and recent infarction and monitor closely if given. (p1311)

front: How does steroid use differ in colonic ischemia and microscopic colitis?
back: Systemic glucocorticoids lack established benefit and increase perforation risk in ischemia. Budesonide can induce remission in microscopic colitis. (p1306, p1310)

front: Why can an elevated PSA be difficult to interpret?
back: Benign enlargement, inflammation and infection can raise it. Conversely, a value below 4 ng/mL cannot exclude cancer. (p1412)

front: What information should influence the decision to investigate a possible localized tumor?
back: Life expectancy, comorbidity, tumor risk, patient preferences and the effect of diagnosis and treatment on baseline quality of life. (p1409–1412)

front: How do active surveillance and watchful waiting differ?
back: Surveillance monitors for progression while preserving an option for curative treatment. Watchful waiting anticipates palliation if symptoms develop. (p1414)

front: What surveillance schedule is described in the book?
back: PSA every three months, DRE every six months and further biopsy as warranted by findings. (p1414)

front: Which patient features support considering radical prostatectomy?
back: Organ-confined disease, life expectancy exceeding ten years and absence of surgical contraindications, considered with treatment preferences. (p1414)

front: What can a new severe backache signal in prostate cancer?
back: Spinal cord compression. Pain often precedes neurologic deficits, so a normal examination does not settle the question. (p1416)

front: What needs evaluation when a weight-bearing bone metastasis becomes painful?
back: Risk of impending fracture. Arrange timely orthopedic or radiation assessment alongside pain management. (p1416)

front: What is the therapeutic aim of ADT in advanced hormone-sensitive disease?
back: Reduce testosterone stimulation of cancer growth. Medical or surgical castration can achieve this and help palliate symptomatic disease. (p1416)

front: Why cover an LHRH agonist with an antiandrogen in metastatic disease?
back: An initial testosterone surge can worsen symptoms. The book starts coverage seven to ten days beforehand and continues it for at least thirty days in total. (p1416)

front: Which skeletal consequence of ADT is distinct from metastasis?
back: Reduced bone mineral density with an increased fracture risk. Consider bone-density testing and measures to protect bone health. (p1417)

front: Which bisphosphonate has demonstrated benefit for bone metastases in the chapter's comparison?
back: Zoledronic acid. The comparison is among bisphosphonates tested in advanced prostate cancer. (p1418)

front: What should be assessed before zoledronic acid?
back: Renal function and dental health, because renal toxicity and osteonecrosis of the jaw are concerns. (p1418)

front: What does denosumab target, and what outcome did the comparison assess?
back: It targets RANK ligand. The comparison with zoledronic acid assessed prevention of skeletal-related events in men with metastatic castration-resistant disease. (p1418)

front: How do the book's descriptions of docetaxel and mitoxantrone differ?
back: Docetaxel demonstrated survival benefit in castration-resistant disease. Mitoxantrone with prednisone can palliate symptoms without a demonstrated survival advantage. (p1418)

front: How can local radiotherapy help a patient on systemic treatment?
back: It can relieve focal bone pain and may help prevent an impending pathologic fracture. Local and systemic treatment serve different purposes. (p1419)

front: What is the difference between fatigue and fatigability?
back: Fatigue is the patient's symptom. Fatigability relates that symptom to a defined activity, such as a standardized walking task. (p1072–1073)

front: What should a fatigue history establish before testing?
back: Onset, pattern, activities that worsen or relieve symptoms, effect on life and relationships, sleep, mood and medication exposure. (p1073)

front: What important acute causes can present as new fatigue?
back: Myocardial infarction or heart failure can present this way. The rest of the history and examination guide testing for anemia, infection and other systemic causes. (p1073)

front: What limits enthusiasm for psychostimulants in fatigue?
back: Trial results are inconsistent. Hypertension and tachycardia are important potential harms, especially with cardiovascular disease or arrhythmia. (p1073)

front: Whose report best measures breathlessness when it is available?
back: The patient's. Oxygen saturation, carbon dioxide and respiratory rate may not track how breathless the person feels. (p1073)

front: How can an activity-based breathlessness scale improve assessment?
back: It connects the symptom to a concrete task, such as walking on a hill or dressing, and helps show the effect on function. (p1074)

front: What three broad mechanisms can cause breathlessness?
