back: Cost, lack of information, stigma or access barriers may prevent use. Confirm what happened and adjust the arrangement if it failed. (p278–279)

front: Which concerns become more apparent during a home visit?
back: Home conditions, practical safety, caregiver demands, finances, medication use and how the patient adapts to illness in daily life. (p279)

front: How can a community social worker reach people beyond those receiving individual counseling?
back: Through community education, consultation, group programs, service development and work on local policy. (p280)

front: What should be established before relying on a family discharge plan?
back: What care is needed, who is available and able to provide it, and what additional services can actually be arranged. (p280–281)

front: What can social work contribute after a person enters long-term care?
back: Assess adjustment and psychosocial needs, advocate for the resident and work with staff and family as care needs or relationships change. (p280)

front: Which hospice tasks extend beyond locating services?
back: Facilitating family communication, addressing emotional and spiritual concerns, supporting transitions and helping relatives through loss and bereavement. (p281)

front: Why ask an immigrant about language and personal history instead of inferring needs from nationality?
back: Experiences vary with language proficiency, reasons for migration, resources and time spent in the country. Those details change what help is accessible. (p281–282)

front: Why might someone entering residential care conceal a long-standing relationship?
back: Prior discrimination or fear of unequal treatment can make disclosure feel unsafe. Ask whom the person wants involved and protect their privacy. (p282–283)

front: Which warning signs might prompt assessment of neglect?
back: Poor nutrition or hygiene, pressure wounds, inadequate access to medical care or unsafe living conditions. Explore circumstances, safety and available support. (p283–284)

front: What does a dementia assessment need beyond a cognitive test?
back: Information about function at home, the physical and social environment, family relationships, available resources and legal or advance-planning needs. (p284)

front: Why explore alcohol or other substance use in a newly isolated older adult?
back: Loss, pain or isolation may contribute to misuse. Changes in mood or function can otherwise be misattributed to aging or cognitive illness. (p285)

front: Who was represented by the poll described in this chapter?
back: US adults aged 50–80, with some reports limited to particular age or symptom groups. Interpret each question using its own denominator. (p287)

front: What mismatch did the brain-health poll bring to light?
back: Many respondents worried about dementia but few aged 50–64 had discussed prevention with a physician, even among those with a family history. (p287–288)

front: How can care from several prescribers or pharmacies affect medication review?
back: Each clinician or pharmacist may see an incomplete list. Reconstruct what the patient actually takes, including nonprescription items. (p288)

front: Why ask about leftover antibiotics?
back: Some respondents saved them for a future illness or another person. Ask how they intend to use or dispose of them and explain appropriate use. (p288–289)

front: Which topics were less often discussed than opioid dosing frequency?
back: Adverse effects, when to reduce the dose, overdose and addiction. Include storage and disposal of leftovers in the conversation. (p289–290)

front: What can the marijuana poll tell a clinician about pain treatment?
back: What respondents believed about pain relief and whether they disclosed use. It cannot establish the efficacy of an analgesic. (p290)

front: Which two urinary-leakage estimates have different denominators?
back: Among surveyed women, 46% reported leakage in the prior year. Among those reporting leakage, 31% had episodes almost daily. (p291)

front: What commonly kept women from raising urinary leakage with a clinician?
back: Many felt it was not serious enough, had other issues to discuss or did not consider it a health problem. (p291–292)

front: What might be missed if a clinician assumes a patient is asking for another test?
back: The patient may be concerned about harm, cost or unnecessary testing. Discuss what the result would change and why a test may offer little benefit. (p292)

front: Why distinguish the offer of telehealth from actual uptake?
back: A service can be available while technology, privacy or the need for an examination makes a visit difficult to use. (p293)

front: What did the poll find about costs before Medicare age?
back: Among respondents aged 50–64, 13% had gone without medical care because of cost in the previous year. Employer insurance also influenced retirement decisions. (p294)

front: What are the three forms of everyday ageism discussed?
back: Ageist messages in the environment, ageism in interactions and ageist beliefs a person comes to hold about themself. (p295)

front: What is the financial dimension of food insecurity?
back: Difficulty obtaining food because money is short. Ask about access to food and use of assistance programs. (p296)

front: Which emergency-preparedness question matters particularly for electrically powered medical equipment?
back: Ask about backup power. In the relevant poll subgroup, only 25% reported an alternative source. (p297)

front: How should the 2020 finding on isolation be interpreted?
back: It describes self-reported isolation during the early pandemic compared with before it. Individual experiences varied, including respondents reporting no change. (p299)

front: Why do some less-developed countries face a compressed timetable for adapting to population aging?
back: Their older populations are growing rapidly and in large absolute numbers, while health and social systems also face other priorities. (p179)

front: How does falling fertility interact with longer survival?
back: There are fewer working-age adults relative to older people who may need support. Wealth and service arrangements affect what that means in practice. (p179)

front: Why can treatment of each named disease leave disability unaddressed?
back: Multimorbidity, cognitive problems, environment and functional limitations interact. Treating one pathology may not restore daily function. (p179–180)

front: Which historical observation helped establish geriatric medicine?
back: Some people regarded as chronically disabled had treatable illnesses or function that improved with assessment and rehabilitation. (p180)

front: How were the international data collected?
back: National leaders reported on training, practice and support in 63 countries. Definitions and availability of information varied. (p181)

front: Which income group was missing from the survey?
back: No low-income country responded. Generalizing findings to its health systems therefore requires care. (p181)

front: What does the nearly 90% figure describe?
back: The fraction of responding countries reporting formal geriatric training programs. It is not the fraction of older adults with access to a geriatrician. (p181)

front: What varies even when two countries both certify geriatricians?
back: Entry after medical school or another specialty, training duration and the use of a standardized examination may differ. (p181–186)

front: What denominator and model underlie the Royal College workforce estimate?
back: Two per 100,000 people aged 75 or older, assuming a consultative model. The workforce table uses a different age cutoff. (p181, p183)

front: Why can the same number of specialists imply different access to care?
back: Specialists may provide direct continuing care or consult for primary clinicians, and their distribution across cities and rural areas varies. (p181, p186)

front: What is the most common setting for specialist geriatric practice in the survey?
back: Hospital practice, often concentrated in larger urban or academic hospitals. (p186)

front: Who commonly provides medical care to residents of long-term care facilities?
back: General practitioners in many settings. Some jurisdictions use geriatricians as primary physicians or consultants. (p181, p186)

front: What does interRAI contribute to comparisons of care?
back: Common assessments support comparisons of function, service use, outcomes and quality across sites and settings. (p181)

front: Which country example illustrates compatible home and long-term care assessments?
back: New Zealand used interRAI in both settings. Compatible instruments can also support communication across services. (p181, p189)

front: How can a country expand geriatric capacity beyond training more physicians?
back: Train other disciplines and improve referral, assessment and service organization across settings. Several countries described geriatric certification in other professions. (p181, p189)

front: Which two demographic changes increase the proportion of older adults?
back: Declining fertility reduces the relative number of younger people, and improving survival allows more people to reach advanced ages. (p23–25)

front: What does rectangularization of the survival curve describe?
back: More of the population surviving until late life before deaths become concentrated at older ages. (p25)

front: What would constitute compression of morbidity?
back: A later onset of morbidity or disability relative to the end of life, concentrating the period lived with illness or disability nearer death. (p26)

front: Why use remaining life expectancy for someone already aged 65?
back: That person has survived risks occurring before that age. A figure calculated at birth includes those earlier deaths. (p25–26)

front: How does a cohort effect differ from a period effect?
back: A cohort shares exposures associated with its birth period. A period effect reflects an event or circumstance experienced across age groups at a particular time. (p26–27)

front: Why is the age-based dependency ratio an imperfect estimate of financial burden?
back: Many people classified by age as dependent still work, and assets and transfers also affect dependence. (p27–28)

front: Which chronic condition was most common among older Medicare beneficiaries in the chapter?
back: Hypertension. The distribution derives from a particular covered population, and several conditions can coexist in one person. (p29–31)

front: How do comorbidity and multimorbidity differ?
back: Comorbidity is considered relative to an index disease. Multimorbidity describes multiple conditions without designating one as primary. (p31)

front: What age contrast in US multiple chronic conditions did the chapter report for 2018?
back: 64% among adults 65 or older, compared with 33% among adults 45–64. (p31)

front: Why can shopping reveal difficulty before a person needs help dressing?
back: Shopping is an instrumental activity that combines mobility, planning and community access. Dressing is a basic self-care task. (p33)

front: What three types of performance does the SPPB sample?
back: Standing balance, gait speed over 4 meters and repeated chair stands as a measure of lower-extremity strength. (p34)

front: How do progressive and catastrophic disability differ?
back: One develops gradually. The other can begin suddenly after an acute event such as a stroke. (p37)

front: Why repeat functional assessment after an episode of disability?
back: Disability can improve and recur. Measuring only at onset may wrongly imply permanent dependence. (p36–37)

front: Why interpret a near-perfect cognitive screening score cautiously?
back: A ceiling effect can obscure subtle differences. Education, the domains assessed and physical or sensory function affect interpretation. (p39–40)

front: How can a neighborhood change disability without changing a diagnosis?
back: Transport, street design and social resources can facilitate or restrict activity and participation for someone with the same underlying impairment. (p43–44)

front: Why does the life-course view avoid a fixed psychosocial threshold for old age?
back: Biology, culture, personal history and resources lead to different transitions at different times. (p65–67)

front: What does socioemotional selectivity predict as the perceived time horizon shortens?
back: Present-oriented and emotionally meaningful goals gain importance, often favoring close familiar relationships. (p68, p72)

front: A patient's social network has become smaller. What would establish whether this is a problem?
back: Ask whether the person feels lonely, has the relationships they want and can obtain practical or emotional support when needed. (p68–69)

front: How can selection, optimization and compensation preserve valued activities?
back: Choose a priority, invest available time and effort in it and adapt the way it is carried out when earlier abilities decline. (p73)

front: What shapes how much help an older parent receives?
back: The parent's needs, the family's resources and relationships, formal services and the wider cultural and policy context. (p69)

front: What is resilience in the chapter's account of stress?
back: The ability to recover from or benefit from adversity, drawing on personal coping resources and available support. (p70–71)

front: Why ask about repeated small losses as well as major life events?
back: Persistent strain and accumulated losses can exceed coping or regulatory capacity even without one dramatic precipitant. (p70–71)

front: What did the women's disability study add to interpretation of age and mood?
back: Depressed mood was more common with greater functional limitation. Age alone cannot explain the pattern of emotional well-being. (p72–73)

front: What needs assessment when someone wants to stay in their own home?
back: How the built environment, available help and community services fit changing functional needs and the person's preferences. (p73–76)

front: How might a village or community program support aging in place?
back: By connecting people with practical assistance, social participation and local services that make daily life at home feasible. (p75–77)

front: Which circumstances make adjustment to retirement easier?
back: More control over the decision, adequate income and health, and opportunities for meaningful roles after retirement. (p78)

front: Why ask a surviving spouse about events before the death?
back: Strain, caregiving demands and the experience of end-of-life care can influence bereavement and the support the survivor needs. (p78–79)

front: What should be checked when a patient appears disengaged from a decision?
back: Whether information was understandable and accessible despite sensory, physical or cognitive barriers, and how the patient wishes to take part. (p78–79)

front: How does valuation of life differ from a health-status score?
back: It addresses what makes continuing life worthwhile to that person. Health limitations alone do not disclose meaning or quality of life. (p79)

front: What is the purpose of the narrative produced in dignity therapy?
back: To help a person with life-limiting illness reflect on what matters in their life and leave a personal account to share if they choose. (p80)

front: Why was Swedish life expectancy of 18 years in 1773 a misleading guide to the usual age of adult death?
back: About half the deaths were before age five. Many people who reached adulthood lived into their forties and fifties. (p83)

front: What does a period life expectancy combine?
back: The mortality rates of different age groups in one period, drawn from people born in different years. It is not the observed lifetime of a single birth cohort. (p83–84)

front: What early-life observation supports a biological contribution to the survival difference?
back: Female infants generally had better survival even in settings and eras where better care for girls was unlikely to explain it. (p85)

front: Why express a life-expectancy gap both in years and as a percentage?
back: The same absolute difference represents a larger proportional gap when average lifespan is shorter. (p86)

front: How can smoking affect a changing national sex gap?
back: Men and women took up and stopped smoking at different times. Later differences in smoking-related mortality altered the gap across cohorts. (p86–87)

front: Which feature of a log mortality plot measures demographic aging in this chapter?
back: The rate at which age-specific mortality rises, represented by the slope. Vertical separation signals a difference in mortality level. (p84–85, p87)

front: Can men's and women's demographic aging rates be similar if men die younger?
back: Yes. Mortality can be higher in men at each age even when it increases at a similar proportional rate with advancing age. (p87)

front: What does the example of first myocardial infarction illustrate?
back: In the US data, women's first infarction occurred about 8 years later on average. Later onset does not guarantee better survival after an infarct. (p89)

front: Why distinguish cause-specific rates from percentages of all deaths?
back: The percentage depends on competing causes and the population's age distribution. Age-adjusted rates allow a different comparison. (p88–90)

front: Why are death certificates problematic for comparing dementia across decades?
back: Recognized diagnoses and how chronic illness is recorded as a cause of death can change, in addition to changes in actual risk. (p89–90)

front: How does Alzheimer disease qualify the usual female advantage in mortality?
back: Women live longer and the chapter also describes greater susceptibility. Longevity alone does not account for its US mortality pattern. (p90)

front: How do reproductive hormone trajectories differ in later life?
back: Menopause entails a relatively abrupt fall in ovarian hormones, whereas testosterone generally declines more gradually in men. (p90)

front: Does hormone replacement establish a general longevity benefit in the groups reviewed?
back: The chapter describes mixed disease-specific effects in women and limited benefits for age-related problems in normal older men. It does not establish general life extension. (p90)

front: What is the health-survival paradox?
back: Women tend to survive longer while often reporting more symptoms, functional limitations and health-service use than men. (p92–93)

front: Why examine variation between US counties when considering sex and longevity?
back: Income, education, behavior and access to care vary geographically and can change the size and trajectory of the gap within one country. (p90–92)

front: Which domains belong to the chapter's social-determinants framework?
back: Economic stability, education, health care, neighborhood and built environment, and the social or community context. (p95–96)

front: How does the chapter define a health disparity?
back: A difference in health outcomes arising from unjust or inequitable conditions, particularly those affecting disadvantaged populations. (p97–98)

front: What does pursuing health equity require beyond describing a difference?
back: Identifying and addressing barriers to optimal health, with attention to people historically excluded from opportunities and resources. (p97–98)

front: How can a housing hazard involve more than one level of influence?
back: An individual may see the risk while a lease limits modifications, local affordable options are scarce and public policy shapes housing access. (p96–97)

front: Why should race not be used as the biological mechanism for a disparity?
back: It is a social construct. Racism and unequal exposure to resources, hazards or treatment can affect health through identifiable pathways. (p97–99)

front: What does intersectionality add to an assessment?
back: It asks how interacting identities and systems of disadvantage shape this individual's experience, beyond any one group label. (p98, p100)

front: How could historical mortgage discrimination affect health decades later?
back: Restrictions on credit and homeownership shaped where people could live, accumulated household wealth and access to neighborhood opportunities. (p99)

front: How does the weathering hypothesis complement a sensitive-period explanation?
back: Weathering emphasizes accumulated exposure to structural disadvantage. The developmental view emphasizes the importance of timing during vulnerable life stages. (p100)

front: How can an open-ended life story reveal a current health barrier?
back: Asking about past work, home, community and relationships can reveal financial constraints, unsafe conditions or sources of support that a checklist misses. (p101–103)

front: Why might assessment reasonably take several visits?
back: Sensitive experiences may need trust and time. Spreading the discussion can reduce burden and allow the person to choose what to disclose. (p102)

front: What else should be elicited alongside discrimination and health risks?
back: Coping strategies, health-promoting behavior, strengths and the people or communities that support the patient. (p101–102)

front: How should the clinician establish who belongs in a conversation about care?
back: Ask whom the patient wants included and how they describe those relationships, using the patient's language and chosen form of address. (p102–103)

front: Why is a positive social-needs screen only the beginning of a referral?
back: The service must exist, be accessible and fit the need. Establish a contact, document the plan and follow up on what happened. (p103–104)

front: When advising someone to stop driving, what consequences should be anticipated?
back: Loss of independent access to appointments, food and social contacts. Ask about chosen supports and workable transportation alternatives. (p104–105)

front: Give an organizational intervention that a single bedside referral cannot accomplish.
back: Build partnerships between clinical and community services, set up a system for follow-up, or change workforce and funding practices that affect access across a population. (p101–104)
